## 10.3 Mechanical Odometers, Two's Complement Arithmetic & Bitwise Masks

### 10.3.1 Two's-Complement Modular Addition

Because a silicon register contains only binary switches that are `1` (ON) or `0` (OFF), representing signed negative integers requires encoding the sign within the bit pattern itself.

Early computer designers in the 1940s tried the obvious idea first: use the leftmost bit as a "sign flag" (`0` for $+$, `1` for $-$) and leave the remaining bits as the ordinary magnitude (Sign-Magnitude representation). That sounds simple until you try to build the adder circuit: to add $+5$ and $-3$, the hardware first has to compare which number is larger, switch from an adder circuit to a subtractor circuit, and resolve two distinct representations of zero (`+0` and `-0`).

Modular arithmetic provides a direct way to represent negative numbers so that an ordinary binary adder can add positive and negative integers together without knowing which operands are negative. A 4-digit mechanical bicycle odometer set to `0000` miles illustrates how modular wrap-around encodes negative values. Riding forward $1\text{ mile}$ advances the rightmost wheel upward to `0001`, whereas starting at `0000` and rolling the wheel backward one mile ($0 - 1 = -1$) wraps all four mechanical number wheels backward one click from `0` to `9` so the odometer window reads `9999`. Rolling backward a second mile ($0 - 2 = -2$) yields `9998`, and rolling backward three miles ($-3$) yields `9997`.

Starting with the odometer at `9997` (the four-digit modular representation of $-3$) and riding forward $5\text{ miles}$ ($+5$) advances the wheels five clicks in sequence through `9998`, `9999`, `0000` (where the carry spills off the left end of the 4-digit window), `0001`, and finally `0002`. By representing $-3$ as $10,000 - 3 = 9997$, ordinary forward addition ($9997 + 0005 = \cancel{1}0002 \to \mathbf{0002}$) automatically computes $(-3) + 5 = +2$ without separate subtraction circuitry.

In binary hardware, that exact odometer wrap-around is called Two's Complement arithmetic. On a 36-bit binary odometer (`000000000h` in nine-nibble hexadecimal), rolling forward from `000000000h` ($0$) counts upward through all positive integers up to `7FFFFFFFFh` ($+2^{35} - 1 = +34,359,738,367$), where the leftmost bit (Bit 35, the Most Significant Bit or `MSB`) is `0` and all 35 lower bits are `1`. Rolling backward one click from `000000000h` ($0 - 1 = -1$) turns every single bit to `1`, displaying `FFFFFFFFFh` in hexadecimal (`36` consecutive `1` bits in binary). The Two's Complement negative ($-X$) of any integer $X$ follows directly from bitwise inversion: on a 36-bit odometer, $X$ plus its bitwise logical inverse $\overline{X}$ (where every `0` flips to `1` and every `1` flips to `0`) always equals a string of thirty-six `1`s (`FFFFFFFFFh`), which is one click below zero ($-1$):

$$X + \overline{X} = \text{FFFFFFFFFh} \equiv -1 \pmod{2^{36}} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad -X = \overline{X} + 1$$

Flipping every bit (`NOT`) and adding $1$ produces the exact additive inverse. That single rule ($\overline{X} + 1$) is how modern microprocessors and the `[+/-]` change-sign key on the SC-32 negate integers on the 36-bit odometer and reduce subtraction ($Y - X = Y + \overline{X} + 1$) to pure addition.

| Bit Position | Field Designation | Meaning in 36-Bit Two's Complement |
| :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Bit 35** | `MSB` / Sign Bit | `0` = Positive integer ($0$ to $+2^{35}-1$); `1` = Negative integer ($-2^{35}$ to $-1$) |
| **Bits 34–32** | Upper Headroom | Provides 3 full bits of positive magnitude headroom ($8\times$ capacity) below Sign Bit 35 |
| **Bits 31–0** | Standard 32-Bit Word | Holds full 32-bit unsigned addresses, IPv4 netmasks, and GPIO bitfields |

### 10.3.2 Cleaving Words at Bit Boundaries via Euclidean Division (`÷R`)

In elementary arithmetic, dividing $12,345$ by $16$ produces a quotient of $771$ with a remainder of $9$, because:

$$12,345 = 771 \times 16 + 9$$

Number theorists call this Euclidean Division ($N = Q \cdot D + R$, with $0 \le R < D$). In algebra class, we often abandon remainders in favor of decimal fractions ($12,345 / 16 = 771.5625$). Yet in computer science, keeping the integer quotient $Q = \lfloor N / D \rfloor$ and the integer remainder $R = N \bmod D$ separate is one of the most versatile operations in mathematics.

Dividing a binary integer $N$ by a power of two $D = 2^k$ via Euclidean division cleaves the binary word in two at bit position $k$. The integer quotient $Q = \lfloor N / 2^k \rfloor$ performs a right bit-shift ($N \gg k$), sliding all upper bits from Bit $k$ upward down by $k$ positions into the ones column and discarding the lower $k$ bits. Simultaneously, the remainder $R = N \bmod 2^k$ forms a bitwise `AND` low-bit mask ($N \ \& \ (2^k - 1)$) that preserves the exact, unshifted value of the lower $k$ bits (`Bits [k-1 : 0]`).

On the SC-32, the dedicated Euclidean division key `[↱] [÷R]` (`[↱]` + `[E]`) models this cleavage directly across the two lower registers of the stack: placing any integer in Register $Y$ and a power-of-two divisor $2^k$ in Register $X$ and pressing `[↱] [÷R]` deposits the right-shifted upper quotient $\lfloor Y / X \rfloor$ into Register $X$ and the masked lower remainder $Y \bmod X$ into Register $Y$ in a single keystroke. In the $12,345 \div 16$ example expressed in hexadecimal, $12,345_{10} = \mathtt{3039h}$ and $16_{10} = 2^4 = \mathtt{10h}$. Dividing $\mathtt{3039h}$ by $\mathtt{10h}$ ($2^4$) via `[↱] [÷R]` places the quotient $Q = \mathtt{303h}$ ($771_{10}$, the upper nibbles shifted right by 4 bits) in Register $X$ and the remainder $R = \mathtt{9h}$ ($9_{10}$, the bottom 4-bit nibble masked off) in Register $Y$.

That single mathematical relationship unifies six classic computer-engineering operations without dedicated bit-shift submenus. Shifting left by $k$ bits ($X \ll k$) multiplies by $M = 2^k$, whereas shifting right by $k$ bits ($X \gg k$) takes the integer quotient on dividing by $M = 2^k$. Masking the lowest $k$ bits ($X \ \& \ (2^k - 1)$) extracts the remainder $X \bmod 2^k$, and snapping an address down to a $2^k$-aligned block ($X \ \& \ \overline{(2^k - 1)}$) takes the quotient $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor$ and multiplies back by $2^k$ to zero out the bottom $k$ bits. Extracting an interior bit-field (`Bits [m : k]`) takes the remainder modulo $2^{m+1}$ to strip bits above bit $m$ and divides by $2^k$ to shift bit $k$ down to bit $0$. Finally, adding $+2^k$ to a register whose $k$-th bit is `0` sets Bit $k$ to `1` (`OR`), while subtracting $2^k$ when Bit $k$ is `1` clears Bit $k$ to `0` (`AND NOT`) without affecting neighboring bits.

### 10.3.3 Euclid's Remainder Ladder: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) and Least Common Multiple (LCM)

Around 300 BCE in Alexandria, Euclid recorded in Book VII, Proposition 2 of his *Elements* what Donald Knuth called the oldest nontrivial algorithm in mathematics: the Euclidean Algorithm for the Greatest Common Divisor $\operatorname{GCD}(a, b)$ of two integers. When a digital signal processor runs one clock domain at $a = 1,071\text{ MHz}$ and another at $b = 462\text{ MHz}$, finding the largest common reference frequency that divides both evenly does not require prime factorization. Euclid noted that any divisor of both $a$ and $b$ must also divide the remainder $R = a \bmod b$ from Euclidean division (`[↱] [÷R]`). Replacing $(a, b)$ with $(b, a \bmod b)$ and pressing `[↱] [÷R]` repeatedly steps down Euclid's Remainder Ladder: $1071 = 2 \times 462 + 147 \longrightarrow 462 = 3 \times 147 + 21 \longrightarrow 147 = 7 \times 21 + 0$. The last non-zero remainder before `0` is $\operatorname{GCD}(1071, 462) = \mathbf{21}$.

On the SC-32, you can either step down Euclid's ladder manually with `[↱] [÷R]` or execute the entire ladder in a single keystroke inside the `[↱] [PARTS]` menu (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[√x]`), which places `[GCD]` (`[LFU4]`) and `[LCM]` (`[LFU5]`) side by side alongside `[IP]`, `[FP]`, `[ABS]`, and `[SGN]`. Once $\operatorname{GCD}(a, b)$ is known, dividing the product $|a \cdot b|$ by $\operatorname{GCD}(a, b)$ gives the Least Common Multiple:

$$\operatorname{LCM}(a, b) = \frac{|a \cdot b|}{\operatorname{GCD}(a, b)}$$

Together, `[GCD]` and `[LCM]` solve three everyday problems across computer engineering and mechanics: reducing gear-tooth or aspect ratios ($1920 \times 1080$ divided by $\operatorname{GCD}(1920, 1080) = 120$ gives the $16:9$ display ratio), finding the exact cycle period $\operatorname{LCM}(T_1, T_2)$ when two asynchronous timer buses realign in phase, and verifying that a public exponent $e$ is coprime to Euler's totient ($\operatorname{GCD}(e, \varphi(n)) = 1$) in RSA public-key cryptography.

### 10.3.4 Real-World Bitwise Engineering: Subnet Masks, RGB Pixels, Base64, Endianness & IEEE-754 Floats

Reading hexadecimal nibbles and cleaving binary words at powers of two ($2^k$) clarifies five foundational operations in digital systems. In IPv4 address slicing and `CIDR` subnetting, every IPv4 address $A$ on the Internet is a single unsigned 32-bit integer written for human convenience in dotted-quad decimal notation $B_3.B_2.B_1.B_0$ as four 8-bit bytes (octets, each ranging from `0` to `255`, or `00h` to `FFh`), packed via Horner's radix-256 polynomial $A = ((B_3 \cdot 256 + B_2)\cdot 256 + B_1)\cdot 256 + B_0$:

| Address Component | Octet 1 (`Bits 31–24`) | Octet 2 (`Bits 23–16`) | Octet 3 (`Bits 15–8`) | Octet 4 (`Bits 7–0`) |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **32-Bit Host IP ($A$)** | $B_3$ ($\times 2^{24}$) | $B_2$ ($\times 2^{16}$) | $B_1$ ($\times 2^8$) | $B_0$ ($\times 2^0$) |
| **`/24` Netmask (`FFFFFF00h`)** | `11111111` (Network) | `11111111` (Network) | `11111111` (Network) | `00000000` (Host) |
| **Aligned `/24` Network Base** | $B_3$ | $B_2$ | $B_1$ | `00000000` (`0`) |

In Classless Inter-Domain Routing (`CIDR`), a `/p` prefix notation specifies that the upper $p$ bits (`Bits [31 : 32-p]`) form the shared Network Prefix, while the remaining $k = 32 - p$ lower bits (`Bits [k-1 : 0]`, spanning $M = 2^k$ addresses per subnet block) identify the individual Host Offset. Dividing a 32-bit address $A$ (or its active boundary octet) by the block stride $M = 2^{32-p}$ via `[↱] [÷R]` cleaves the address right at the subnet boundary: the integer remainder $R = A \bmod 2^k$ isolates the host offset within the block, while multiplying the integer quotient $Q = \lfloor A / 2^k \rfloor$ back by $2^k$ zeroes out the $k$ host bits to snap directly to the aligned network base address $A_{\text{net}} = \lfloor A / 2^k \rfloor \times 2^k$. Adding the inverted host wildcard mask $W = 2^k - 1 = \mathtt{FFFFFFFFh} - \text{Netmask}$ then populates all $k$ host bits with `1`s to form the directed broadcast address $A_{\text{bcast}} = A_{\text{net}} + (2^k - 1)$.

A second application is packing color channels and Base64 characters by Horner's method. A smartwatch or microcontroller color display packs three separate Red, Green, and Blue brightness values into a single 16-bit memory word (`RGB565`). Because the cones in the human retina are most sensitive to subtle shades of green, `RGB565` allocates 5 bits ($R_5 \in [0, 31]$) to Red in `Bits [15:11]`, 6 bits ($G_6 \in [0, 63]$) to Green in `Bits [10:5]`, and 5 bits ($B_5 \in [0, 31]$) to Blue in `Bits [4:0]`:

| Channel Allocation | Bit Positions | Bit Width & Range | Positional Shift Multiplier |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: |
| **Red ($R_5$)** | Bits `15–11` | 5 bits ($0\dots 31$, `00h–1Fh`) | $R_5 \times 2^{11}$ (`× 800h`) |
| **Green ($G_6$)** | Bits `10–5` | 6 bits ($0\dots 63$, `00h–3Fh`) | $G_6 \times 2^5$ (`× 20h`) |
| **Blue ($B_5$)** | Bits `4–0` | 5 bits ($0\dots 31$, `00h–1Fh`) | $B_5 \times 2^0$ (unshifted) |
| **Packed `RGB565` Word** | Bits `15–0` | 16-bit unsigned pixel (`0000h–FFFFh`) | $(R_5 \times \mathtt{800h}) + (G_6 \times \mathtt{20h}) + B_5$ |

Packing the three non-overlapping channels into a single 16-bit integer evaluates $(R_5 \times 2^{11}) + (G_6 \times 2^5) + B_5$, whereas unpacking any 16-bit pixel back into its three color channels requires only two Euclidean divisions (`[↱] [÷R]`) at $2^{11} = \mathtt{800h}$ and $2^5 = \mathtt{20h}$. That same bit-slicing geometry powers Base64 encoding across the web. To transmit binary data over text-only protocols, Base64 welds each group of three 8-bit ASCII bytes $(B_2, B_1, B_0)$ into a single 24-bit integer ($3 \times 8 = 24\text{ bits}$) and slices it at $2^{18} = \mathtt{40000h}$, $2^{12} = \mathtt{1000h}$, and $2^6 = \mathtt{40h}$ into four 6-bit sextet indices ($4 \times 6 = 24\text{ bits}$, each ranging from $0$ to $63$) that map onto the 64 printable characters `A–Z`, `a–z`, `0–9`, `+`, and `/`.

A fourth operation concerns Big-Endian versus Little-Endian byte order and Internet checksums. In 1980, computer scientist Danny Cohen borrowed the terms Big-Endian and Little-Endian from Jonathan Swift's *Gulliver's Travels* (where two empires went to war over whether to crack a soft-boiled egg at the big end or the little end) to describe how computers store multi-byte integers in memory. Network cables transmit bytes Big-Endian (`12345678h`, most-significant byte `12h` first), whereas x86 and ARM processors store bytes Little-Endian (`78563412h`, least-significant byte `78h` first). When routers verify that a packet was not corrupted in flight, they use RFC 1071 16-bit one's-complement addition with end-around carry *([Knuth, 1997](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-knuth1997))*, dividing the 32-bit accumulated sum by $2^{16} = \mathtt{10000h}$ and adding the upper carry quotient right back into the lower 16-bit remainder, because end-around carry produces the identical checksum on both Big-Endian and Little-Endian machines.

Finally, to store a real number $x$ inside a fixed-width binary word, William Kahan's IEEE-754 floating-point standard *([IEEE, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-ieee754_2019); [Golub & Van Loan, 1996](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-golub1996); [Parker, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-parker2019))* factors every normal non-zero value into normalized base-2 scientific notation with an implicit leading `1.` bit before the binary point:

$$x = (-1)^S \times 2^{E - \text{bias}} \times \left(1 + \frac{M}{2^p}\right)$$

Because every non-zero normalized binary significand begins with `1.`, IEEE-754 omits that hidden bit from storage to gain one extra bit of precision. A 32-bit single-precision float (`binary32`, $p = 23$, $\text{bias} = 127$) packs 1 Sign bit $S$ in `Bit 31`, an 8-bit Biased Exponent $E = e + 127$ in `Bits [30:23]`, and the 23-bit Fractional Mantissa $M$ in `Bits [22:0]`, so cleaving the 32-bit word at $2^{23} = \mathtt{800000h}$ and $2^8 = \mathtt{100h}$ via `[↱] [÷R]` unpacks $M$, $E$, and $S$ onto the stack in two operations (while a 64-bit `binary64` double uses $p = 52$ and an 11-bit exponent with $\text{bias} = 1023$, cleaved in its upper 32-bit half at $2^{20} = \mathtt{100000h}$ and $2^{11} = \mathtt{800h}$).

## 10.4 Combinatorics (PROB), Cryptographic Keyspaces, and the Birthday Collision Paradox

Sizing the state space of a digital register, a network topology, or a cryptographic cipher, and determining the collision threshold of random hashes, rests on the four functions inside the SC-32's `[↱] [PROB]` menu: combinations `[Cn,r]`, permutations `[Pn,r]`, factorials `[↰] [x!]`, and the uniform pseudo-random generator `[RAND]`.

### 10.4.1 Ordered Permutations, Unordered Combinations & Pascal's Symmetry

When drawing $r$ items without replacement from $n$ distinct items (such as $n = 16$ hexadecimal digits `0`–`F` or $n = 12$ server racks), the counting law depends on whether the order of selection is significant. When the order of selection matters (such as assigning $r = 4$ distinct hexadecimal nibbles to a 4-stage shift register, or ordering $r = 5$ packet routes out of $n = 12$), there are $n$ choices for the first slot, $n - 1$ for the second, down to $n - r + 1$ for the $r$-th slot, which defines the ordered permutation `[Pn,r]`:

$$P(n, r) = n(n - 1)\cdots(n - r + 1) = \frac{n!}{(n - r)!}$$

Conversely, when order does not matter (such as choosing any subset of $r = 5$ storage drives out of $n = 12$ for a RAID parity group, or wiring every pair of $r = 2$ routers among $n = 7$ ARPANET nodes), dividing $P(n, r)$ by the $r!$ ways to rearrange the chosen subset yields Blaise Pascal's binomial coefficient `[Cn,r]`:

$$C(n, r) = \binom{n}{r} = \frac{P(n, r)}{r!} = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n - r)!}$$

### 10.4.2 Richard von Mises's Birthday Paradox & Cryptographic Hash Collisions

That ratio between $P(N, k)$ and $N^k$ governs a classic result in probability and cybersecurity: Richard von Mises's Birthday Paradox (1939). When $k$ independent items (people in a room, or random packets in a network) are each assigned one of $N$ equally likely labels (such as $N = 365$ calendar days, or $N = 2^b$ possible values of a $b$-bit hash function), first-order intuition suggests that a collision becomes $50\%$ likely only when $k$ approaches $N/2$.

That estimate is far too large because collisions can occur across any of the $\binom{k}{2} = \frac{k(k-1)}{2}$ distinct pairs among the $k$ items. The exact probability $P_{\text{unique}}$ that all $k$ items receive *distinct* labels is the ordered permutation $P(N, k) = N(N-1)\cdots(N-k+1)$ divided by the $N^k$ total unrestricted assignments, and using the first-order Taylor bound $1 - x \approx e^{-x}$ yields the Gaussian collision law:

$$P(\text{at least one collision}) = 1 - \frac{P(N, k)}{N^k} \approx 1 - \exp\!\left(-\frac{k(k - 1)}{2N}\right)$$

Setting $\exp(-k^2 / 2N) = \frac{1}{2}$ shows that the $50\%$ collision threshold scales not with $N$, but with its square root: $k_{50\%} \approx \sqrt{(2\ln 2)\,N} \approx 1.1774\sqrt{N}$. In computer science, that $\sqrt{N}$ scaling is known as the Birthday Bound: when a $b$-bit hash function or database UUID spans $N = 2^b$ possible values, random collisions become likely after roughly $\sqrt{2^b} = 2^{b/2}$ operations, which is $2^{16} = 65,536$ packets for a 32-bit CRC or $2^{32} \approx 4.29 \times 10^9$ blocks for a 64-bit cipher. Modern cryptographic hashes such as SHA-256 therefore use $b = 256\text{ bits}$, which raises the birthday collision threshold to $2^{128} \approx 3.4 \times 10^{38}$ operations.

## 10.5 36-Bit Radix Representations, Boolean Masks & Bitwise Arithmetic

Because the four positional radices (`DEC`, `HEX`, `OCT`, `BIN`), modular two's-complement arithmetic ($\mathbb{Z}/2^{36}\mathbb{Z}$), and Euclidean division ($N = Q \cdot D + R$) operate on the same underlying 36-bit integer words across Registers `T, Z, Y, X`, base conversions and bit-field extractions execute directly on the lower two stack registers (`Y` and `X`) without disturbing values staged in `Z` and `T`.

Switching the active radix mode via `[↰] [BASE]` (`[↰]` + `[×]`) re-formats all four visible registers on screen without altering their binary contents, while `[↱] [÷R]` (`[↱]` + `[E]`) cleaves any word $N$ in Register `Y` at a power-of-two boundary $D = 2^k$ in Register `X` into its right-shifted upper quotient $Q = \lfloor Y / 2^k \rfloor$ in `X` and its masked lower remainder $R = Y \bmod 2^k$ in `Y` (where a single tap of `[x⇄y]` swaps `R` into `X` and `Q` into `Y`).

![Decimal 255 converted in place to hexadecimal FFh on the SC-32 transflective display while preserving all four stack registers.](../assets/manuals/screenshots/sc32_base_hex_logic.png)

### 10.5.1 Radix Modes (DEC, HEX, OCT, BIN) & Direct Hex Entry

Following the classic HP-32SII design, the `[↰] [BASE]` menu (Left Shift `[↰]` on `[×]`, Row 5, Column 3) selects the active display and entry radix across all four stack registers:

| Base System | Keystroke | Screen Suffix | Allowed Character Digits | Example Formatted Display |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Decimal** | `[↰] [BASE] [DEC]` | *(none)* | `0` through `9` | `1042` |
| **Hexadecimal** | `[↰] [BASE] [HEX]` | `h` | `0` through `9`, `A` through `F` | `412h` |
| **Octal** | `[↰] [BASE] [OCT]` | `o` | `0` through `7` | `2022o` |
| **Binary** | `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` | `b` | `0` and `1` | `10000010010b` |

If Register $X$ holds `255` in Decimal mode, pressing `[↰] [BASE] [HEX]` re-renders the register as `FFh`, pressing `[↰] [BASE] [OCT]` shows `377o`, and pressing `[↰] [BASE] [BIN]` shows all eight asserted bits as `11111111b`.

When Hexadecimal mode (`[HEX]`) is active, the top row of primary scientific keys across Row 1 maps onto the printed alpha legends $A$ through $F$: `[√x]` enters $\mathbf{A} = 10_{10}$, `[eˣ]` enters $\mathbf{B} = 11_{10}$, `[LN]` enters $\mathbf{C} = 12_{10}$, `[yˣ]` enters $\mathbf{D} = 13_{10}$, `[1/x]` enters $\mathbf{E} = 14_{10}$, and `[Σ+]` enters $\mathbf{F} = 15_{10}$. Entering `0xDEADBEEF` thus uses the top-row sequence `yˣ 1/x √x yˣ eˣ 1/x 1/x Σ+`. In stack tables, hexadecimal literals such as `C0A80A2D` or `1F` are written in compact hex notation for readability; on the keypad in `HEX` mode, enter `A`–`F` using Row 1 (`√x` through `Σ+`). To apply scientific functions such as square root, natural logarithm, or powers to a hexadecimal value, switch back to Decimal mode (`[↰] [BASE] [DEC]`) first so the top-row keys resume their mathematical roles.

Because the SC-32 preserves all four stack registers across base changes, you can also mix radices in the middle of a calculation without jotting down a single intermediate number. To add a hexadecimal base offset $3\text{A}7_{16}$ to an octal permission mask $452_8$ and read the sum in decimal, enter `3 [√x] 7 [ENTER]` ($935_{10}$) in `[HEX]` mode, switch to `[OCT]` mode to add `452 [+]` ($2261_8$), and switch to `[DEC]` mode to read the combined total $\mathbf{1,201_{10}}$ in Register $X$.

### 10.5.2 Euclidean Division (÷R): Flash Memory Pages, IPv4 Octets & Clock Bus Alignment

Applying Euclidean division `[↱] [÷R]` across Registers $Y$ and $X$ while Registers $Z$ and $T$ remain untouched executes byte-address and IPv4 subnet splits directly on the bottom two registers:

* **16-Byte Cache-Line Row & Offset (`12345 ÷R 16`):** For the byte address $12,345 = 771 \times 16 + 9$ (`0x3039`), keying `12345 [ENTER] 16 [↱] [÷R]` in `[DEC]` mode cleaves at the $2^4 = 16$ bit boundary, placing the 16-byte row quotient $Q = \mathbf{771}$ in Register $X$ and the intra-row byte remainder $R = \mathbf{9}$ in Register $Y$ (where a single tap of `[x⇄y]` parks the quotient `771` in Register $Y$ and brings the remainder `9` into Register $X$).
* **256-Byte Flash Page & Offset (`12345 ÷R 256`):** Mapping that same byte address $12,345$ (`0x3039`) onto a SPI NOR flash chip organized into $2^8 = 256\text{-byte}$ programmable pages, keying `12345 [ENTER] 256 [↱] [÷R]` (followed by `[x⇄y]` when inspecting the offset in $X$ and page in $Y$) cleaves the word right at Bit 8 into Page $48$ ($\lfloor 12,345 / 256 \rfloor = 48$, upper byte `0x30`) and Offset $57$ ($12,345 \bmod 256 = 57$, lower byte `0x39`), since $48 \times 256 + 57 = 12,345$, while Registers $Z$ and $T$ remain at zero.

That same two-register `[↱] [÷R]` cleavage decomposes IPv4 network addresses in base $256$ ($2^8$) and aligns `/28` and `/24` Classless Inter-Domain Routing (`CIDR`) subnets:

* **Base-256 IPv4 Octet Unpacking (`3232235777` $\to$ `192.168.1.1`):** An unsigned 32-bit IPv4 socket address such as `3232235777` (`0xC0A80101`) is a four-digit integer written in base $256$. Keying `3232235777 [ENTER] 256 [↱] [÷R]` in `[DEC]` mode strips off the lowest 8-bit octet `1` into Register $Y$ and leaves the upper 24-bit prefix `12625921` in Register $X$. Repeating `256 [↱] [÷R]` peels off the third octet `1` into $Y$ (with `49320` in $X$), and a third `256 [↱] [÷R]` splits the remaining 16-bit prefix into the first octet `192` in Register $X$ and the second octet `168` in Register $Y$, which displays `192.168.1.1` across the four stack registers (`1, 1, 168, 192`).
* **Aligning a `/28` VLAN Interface (`205` $\to$ Block `192`, Offset `13`):** On a `/28` office subnet (`255.255.255.240`, where $32 - 28 = 4$ host bits give a block stride of $2^4 = 16$ addresses), dividing host octet `205` by `16` via `[↱] [÷R]` places the block index `12` in Register $X$ and the host offset `13` in Register $Y$ ($205 = 12 \times 16 + 13$, with $Z$ and $T$ at zero), and multiplying Register $X$ back by `16` zeroes out the low 4 host bits: keying `205 [ENTER] 16 [↱] [÷R] 16 [×]` snaps directly to the aligned `/28` network base ID `192` (`12 × 16 = 192`).

For a packed 32-bit `/24` workstation address `192.168.10.45` (`C0A80A2Dh`, where `192` $= \mathtt{C0h}$, `168` $= \mathtt{A8h}$, `10` $= \mathtt{0Ah}$, and `45` $= \mathtt{2Dh}$), working in `[HEX]` mode slices at the 8-bit host boundary ($2^8 = \text{100h}$) while Registers $Z$ and $T$ rest at `0h`:

* **Align the `/24` Network Base (`192.168.10.0`):** Cleaving `C0A80A2Dh` by `100h` separates the 24-bit network prefix `C0A80Ah` in Register $X$ from the 8-bit host ID `2Dh` ($45_{10}$) in Register $Y$, and multiplying Register $X$ back by `100h` zeros out the host byte. Keying `C0A80A2D [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] 100 [×]` produces the aligned `/24` network base `C0A80A00h` (`192.168.10.0`).
* **Isolate the Inverted Host Wildcard Mask (`0.0.0.255`):** Subtracting the `/24` netmask `FFFFFF00h` from the 32-bit all-ones broadcast word `FFFFFFFFh` flips every network bit to `0` and every host bit to `1`. Keying `FFFFFFFF [ENTER] FFFFFF00 [-]` isolates the 8-bit host wildcard mask `FFh`.
* **Populate the Directed `/24` Broadcast Address (`192.168.10.255`):** Because the aligned network base (`C0A80A00h`) and the host wildcard (`000000FFh`) occupy non-overlapping bit lanes, adding them performs an exact carry-free bitwise `OR` across the bottom 8 bits. Keying `C0A80A00 [ENTER] FF [+]` delivers the directed `/24` broadcast address `C0A80AFFh`.

### 10.5.3 36-Bit Two's Complement Odometer Seams & Hardware Bit-Fields

The two rollover seams of the 36-bit two's-complement odometer ($\mathbb{Z}/2^{36}\mathbb{Z}$) appear directly in `[HEX]` mode on Registers $Y$ and $X$ *([Parker, 2019](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-parker2019))*:

* **Signed Positive Overflow Seam (`+Max + 1 → -Min`):** At the highest positive 36-bit integer `7FFFFFFFFh` ($+2^{35} - 1 = +34,359,738,367_{10}$), Sign Bit 35 is `0` while all 35 magnitude bits (Bits 34–0) are `1`. Adding `1` propagates a ripple carry through all 35 magnitude bits into Sign Bit 35: keying `7FFFFFFFF [ENTER] 1 [+]` wraps discontinuously to the most negative 36-bit integer `800000000h` ($-2^{35} = -34,359,738,368_{10}$).
* **Zero Underflow Seam (`0 - 1 → -1`):** Decrementing the 36-bit register by one from `0` borrows across every bit position simultaneously and sets all thirty-six bits ON: keying `0 [ENTER] 1 [-]` produces `FFFFFFFFFh` ($-1_{10}$).

Every bit-field shift and mask operation maps directly to a power of two $M = 2^k$ *([Shannon, 1938](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-shannon1938))*:

| Bit-Field / Masking Operation | Mathematical Equivalent ($M = 2^k$) | SC-32 RPN Keystrokes (`HEX` / `DEC`) | Result Location |
| :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- |
| **Left Shift ($X \ll k$)** | $X \times 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [×]` | Shifted word in **`X`** |
| **Right Shift ($X \gg k$)** | $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R]` (or `[÷]` in `HEX`/`OCT`/`BIN`) | Upper bits in **`X`** |
| **Low-Bit Mask ($X \ \& \ (2^k - 1)$)** | $X \bmod 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` | Low $k$ bits in **`X`** |
| **High-Bit Alignment ($X \ \& \ \sim(2^k - 1)$)** | $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor \times 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [↱] [÷R] M [×]` | Aligned base in **`X`** |
| **Set Disjoint Bit $k$** | $X + 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [+]` | Updated word in **`X`** |
| **Clear Set Bit $k$** | $X - 2^k$ | `X [ENTER] M [-]` | Updated word in **`X`** |
| **32-Bit Unsigned Complement** | $\text{FFFFFFFF}_{16} - X$ | `FFFFFFFF [ENTER] X [-]` | Inverted mask in **`X`** |

*(For right bit-shifts in `[DEC]` mode, `[↱] [÷R]` is preferred over `[÷]` because `[÷]` retains fractional decimal digits in Decimal mode, whereas `[↱] [÷R]` always truncates to the integer quotient $\lfloor X / 2^k \rfloor$ in every base.)*

Memory-mapped microcontroller peripherals pack independent hardware control lines into a single register word so firmware can toggle GPIO pins, isolate telemetry fault masks, and extract ADC bit-fields via positional masks $2^k$ without disturbing neighboring lines:

* **Asserting an Unset GPIO Direction Pin (`GPIO_DIR | (1 << 5)`):** When a 32-bit GPIO direction register holds `0x00001804`—meaning Pins 2 ($2^2 = \text{4h}$), 11 ($2^{11} = \text{800h}$), and 12 ($2^{12} = \text{1000h}$) are already configured as outputs while Pin 5 is currently an input (`0`)—adding the unasserted Bit 5 positional weight $2^5 = 32_{10} = \text{20h}$ in `[HEX]` mode performs a carry-free bitwise `OR`: keying `1804 [ENTER] 20 [+]` asserts Pin 5 to produce `1824h` (`1824h`).
* **Clearing and Re-Asserting an Active Heartbeat Pin (`PORT & ~(1 << 2)`):** If a port output register holds `0x00000017` ($0001\,0111_2$) with an active heartbeat line on Bit 2 ($2^2 = \text{4h}$), subtracting the bit weight in `[HEX]` mode performs a borrow-free `AND NOT`: keying `17 [ENTER] 4 [-]` clears Bit 2 to `13h`, and adding `4h` back via `13 [ENTER] 4 [+]` (or `[↰] [LASTX] [+]`) re-asserts the pin to `17h` without disturbing neighboring pins.
* **Isolating Tripped Telemetry Fault Flags (`Status ^ Baseline`):** Whenever a baseline register's asserted bits are a subset of an active status word, borrow-free subtraction acts as an exact bitwise `XOR` difference mask. Comparing a spacecraft downlink status word `0x5F5A` against its nominal baseline `0x5A50` via `5F5A [ENTER] 5A50 [-]` strips away the nominal bits to isolate the newly tripped fault mask `50Ah`, which renders as $\mathbf{10100001010\text{b}}$ in `[BIN]` with a Hamming weight of $4\text{ fault bits}$ at positions 1, 3, 8, and 10.
* **Extracting an Interior Multi-Bit Field (`Bits [7:4]` of `0x3C6A`):** For the 16-bit word `0x3C6A`, when an ADC control register packs a 4-bit oversampling selector in Bits [7:4] (`6h`), extracting that interior field combines a modulo mask ($\bmod 2^8 = \text{100h}$) with an integer right-shift ($\div 2^4 = \text{10h}$):

$$\text{Bits } [7:4] = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathtt{3C6Ah} \bmod 2^8}{2^4} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{\mathtt{6Ah}}{\mathtt{10h}} \right\rfloor = \mathtt{6h}$$

  First, cleaving at $2^8 = \text{100h}$ via `3C6A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` masks off the upper configuration byte (`3Ch`) and brings the lower 8-bit byte `6Ah` into Register $X$; second, right-shifting by 4 bits ($\div 2^4 = \text{10h}$) via `6A [ENTER] 10 [÷]` discards the bottom nibble (`Ah`) so Bits [7:4] land right-justified at Bit 0 as `6h`:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `3C6A [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3C6Ah` | `3C6Ah` | Stage 16-bit ADC register word `3C6Ah` |
| `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `6Ah` | `3Ch` | Split upper byte `3Ch` into X and lower byte `6Ah` into Y |
| `[x⇄y]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3Ch` | `6Ah` | Swap lower byte `6Ah` (Bits [7:0]) into Register X |
| `10 [÷]` | `0h` | `0h` | `3Ch` | `6h` | Shift right by 4 bits (`÷ 10h`) to isolate Bits [7:4] = `6h` |

### 10.5.4 Packing RGB565 Pixels, Slicing Base64 Sextets & Reversing Endianness

Executing `RGB565` pixel packing $(R_5 \times 2^{11}) + (G_6 \times 2^5) + B_5$ for 5-bit Red (`1Fh` $= 31/31$), 6-bit Green (`15h` $= 21/63$), and 5-bit Blue (`06h` $= 6/31$) in `[HEX]` mode shifts and merges the three non-overlapping bit lanes across Registers $Y$ and $X$:

* **Shift Red into `Bits [15:11]` (`× 800h`):** Multiplying Red (`1Fh`) by $2^{11} = \text{800h}$ left-shifts those 5 bits across the Green and Blue lanes: keying `1F [ENTER] 800 [×]` places `F800h` in Register $X$.
* **Shift Green into `Bits [10:5]` (`× 20h`) and Merge:** Multiplying Green (`15h`) by $2^5 = \text{20h}$ via `15 [ENTER] 20 [×]` left-shifts the 6 green bits into Bits [10:5] as `2A0h` while `F800h` waits in Register $Y$.
* **Combine All Three Lanes (`FAA6h`):** Merging Red and Green (`FAA0h`) and adding the unshifted 5-bit Blue channel (`06h`) in Bits [4:0] via `FAA0 [ENTER] 6 [+]` completes the packed 16-bit framebuffer pixel `FAA6h`:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `1F [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `1Fh` | `1Fh` | Stage 5-bit Red channel `1Fh` ($31_{10}$) |
| `800 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `F800h` | Shift Red left 11 bits (`× 800h`) into Bits [15:11] |
| `15 [ENTER]` | `0h` | `F800h` | `15h` | `15h` | Stage 6-bit Green channel `15h` ($21_{10}$); Red lifts to Z |
| `20 [×]` | `0h` | `0h` | `F800h` | `2A0h` | Shift Green left 5 bits (`× 20h`) into Bits [10:5] |
| `[+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `FAA0h` | Combine shifted Red and Green channels (`FAA0h`) |
| `6 [+]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | `FAA6h` | Add 5-bit Blue channel `06h` for packed `RGB565` word `FAA6h` |

Conversely, given a packed 16-bit RGB565 pixel `0xF38E` in `[HEX]` mode, keying `F38E [ENTER] 800 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 20 [↱] [÷R]` unpacks all three color channels onto the visible stack in one pass: Red in Register $Z$ (`1Eh` $= 30_{10}$), Green in Register $X$ (`1Ch` $= 28_{10}$), and Blue in Register $Y$ (`Eh` $= 14_{10}$).

Similarly, slicing the 24-bit ASCII word `"Man"` (`'M' = 4Dh`, `'a' = 61h`, `'n' = 6Eh` $\implies \mathtt{4D616Eh}$) into its four 6-bit Base64 indices cleaves at $2^{18} = \text{40000h}$, $2^{12} = \text{1000h}$, and $2^6 = \text{40h}$ in `[HEX]` mode:

* **Sextet 1 (`Bits [23:18]` $\to$ `'T'`):** Right-shifting by 18 bits (`÷ 40000h`) via `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [÷]` extracts `13h` ($19_{10} \implies$ Base64 `'T'`).
* **Sextet 2 (`Bits [17:12]` $\to$ `'W'`):** Masking the 18-bit remainder and right-shifting by 12 bits (`÷ 1000h`) via `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [÷]` isolates `16h` ($22_{10} \implies$ `'W'`).
* **Sextet 3 (`Bits [11:6]` $\to$ `'F'`):** Cleaving the 12-bit remainder at 6 bits (`÷ 40h`) via `4D616E [ENTER] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [÷]` extracts `5h` ($5_{10} \implies$ `'F'`).
* **Sextet 4 (`Bits [5:0]` $\to$ `'u'`):** Masking the final 6-bit remainder via `4D616E [ENTER] 40 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` leaves `2Eh` ($46_{10} \implies$ `'u'`), spelling out `TWFu`:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [÷]` | `0h` | `0h` | `0h` | **`13h`** | Sextet 1: `4D616Eh >> 18 = 13h` ($19_{10} \implies \mathbf{T}$) |
| `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [÷]` | `13h` | `13h` | `13h` | **`16h`** | Sextet 2: remainder `>> 12 = 16h` ($22_{10} \implies \mathbf{W}$) |
| `4D616E [ENTER] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [÷]` | `16h` | `16h` | `4D6h` | **`5h`** | Sextet 3: remainder `>> 6 = 5h` ($5_{10} \implies \mathbf{F}$) |
| `4D616E [ENTER] 40 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y]` | `4D6h` | `5h` | `13585h` | **`2Eh`** | Sextet 4: lower 6-bit remainder = `2Eh` ($46_{10} \implies \mathbf{u}$) |

*(Single-Entry `÷R` Cascade: Chaining `4D616E [ENTER] 40000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 40 [↱] [÷R]` unpacks all four Base64 indices across the four stack registers—`13h` in $T$, `16h` in $Z$, `2Eh` in $Y$, and `5h` in $X$—with `4D616E` keyed only once.)*

Reversing the 32-bit Big-Endian network header `0x12345678` into its Little-Endian x86/ARM memory representation `0x78563412` (`BSWAP` / `REV`) in `[HEX]` mode folds each shifted byte into a running sum on Register $X$ across Registers $Y$ and $X$ while Registers $Z$ and $T$ stay at `0h`:

* **Promote Byte 0 (`78h` $\ll 24$) into Byte 3:** Multiplying `78h` by $2^{24} = \text{1000000h}$ via `12345678 [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 1000000 [×]` yields `78000000h` (`78000000h`).
* **Promote Byte 1 (`56h` $\ll 16$) into Byte 2:** Multiplying `56h` by $2^{16} = \text{10000h}$ via `12345678 [ENTER] 10000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 100 [↱] [÷R] 10000 [×]` positions `560000h` (`560000h`) and merges them into `78560000h`.
* **Promote Byte 2 (`34h` $\ll 8$) into Byte 1:** Multiplying `34h` by $2^8 = \text{100h}$ via `12345678 [ENTER] 1000000 [↱] [÷R] [x⇄y] 10000 [↱] [÷R] 100 [×]` places `3400h` (`3400h`) into Byte 1 (`78563400h`).
* **Demote Byte 3 (`12h` $\gg 24$) into Byte 0:** Right-shifting the original most-significant byte via `12345678 [ENTER] 1000000 [÷]` isolates `12h` (`12h`), so adding `12h` completes the byte-swapped Little-Endian word `78563412h`.

### 10.5.5 RFC 1071 Checksums, Circular Rotations (`ROL`), UART Dividers & IEEE-754 Unpacking

Executing the RFC 1071 16-bit one's-complement end-around carry checksum on an IPv4 header whose ten 16-bit words sum to `2653Dh` in `[HEX]` mode cleaves at the 16-bit boundary $2^{16} = \text{10000h}$ via `2653D [ENTER] 10000 [↱] [÷R]`, separating the upper carry quotient `2h` in Register $X$ from the lower 16-bit sum `653Dh` in Register $Y$ (with $Z = T = \text{0h}$). Pressing `[+]` folds that end-around carry directly into Bit 0 (`653Fh`), and subtracting from the all-ones 16-bit mask `FFFFh` via `FFFF [x⇄y] [-]` inverts every bit to form the one's-complement wire checksum `9AC0h` ($39,616_{10}$ in `[DEC]`).

In cryptographic block ciphers and cyclic redundancy checks, that same two-register end-around carry implements a circular 1-bit left rotation (`ROL 1`) across an 8-bit register boundary ($2^8 = \text{100h}$), where the bit shifted out of Bit 7 wraps around to enter Bit 0 (`0x85` $= 10000101_2 \implies 00001011_2 = \text{0Bh}$):

* **Left-Shift All 8 Bits (`× 2`):** Doubling `85h` via `85 [ENTER] 2 [×]` shifts the byte left by one position to `10Ah` (`10Ah`), pushing the old MSB into Bit 8.
* **Cleave at the 8-Bit Boundary (`÷R 100h`):** Dividing by `100h` via `10A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R]` separates the low 8-bit remainder (`Ah` in Register $Y$) from the Bit 8 carry (`1h` $= \text{1h}$ in Register $X$).
* **Fold the Carry into Bit 0 (`+`):** Adding the carry back into the low byte via `10A [ENTER] 100 [↱] [÷R] [+]` completes the circularly rotated byte `Bh` (`Bh`).

When configuring an asynchronous serial `UART` transceiver from a $f_{\text{clk}} = 150.0\text{ MHz}$ system bus at $115,200\text{ baud}$ with $8\times$ oversampling, hardware fractional baud-rate generators split the ideal divisor $\text{Divider} = \frac{150,000,000}{8 \times 115,200} \approx 162.760417$ into a 16-bit integer mantissa register (`IBRD`) and a 6-bit fixed-point sixty-fourths register (`FBRD` $= \lfloor 64 \times \text{FP} + 0.5 \rfloor$). Switching to `[DEC]` mode and keying `150000000 [ENTER] 8 [÷] 115200 [÷]` yields the exact divisor `162.760416667` in Register $X$. Duplicating that divisor and extracting `[IP]` isolates `IBRD = 162` while swapping to take the fractional part `[FP]` isolates $0.76041667$; multiplying by $64$ and rounding via `[↰] [RND]` converts $48.6667$ to `FBRD = 49` ($49/64 = 0.765625$) in Register $X$ right beside `IBRD = 162` in Register $Y$.

To unpack the 32-bit IEEE-754 single-precision (`binary32`) word `0xC0C80000`—encoding $-6.25_{10} = -110.01_2 = (-1)^1 \times 2^2 \times 1.1001_2$ as $(-1)^S \times 2^{E - 127} \times (1 + M / 2^{23})$—chain two `[↱] [÷R]` cleavages in `[HEX]` mode at the 23-bit mantissa boundary ($2^{23} = \text{800000h}$) and the 8-bit exponent boundary ($2^8 = \text{100h}$). This places the 23-bit significand `480000h` ($4,718,592 / 2^{23} = 0.5625$, or $1.5625$ with the hidden leading `1.`) in Register $Z$, the biased exponent `81h` ($129_{10}$, so $e = 129 - 127 = 2$) in Register $Y$, and the sign bit `1h` in Register $X$ to verify $(-1)^1 \times 2^2 \times 1.5625 = -6.25$:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| `C0C80000 [ENTER]` | `0h` | `0h` | `C0C80000h` | `C0C80000h` | Stage 32-bit IEEE-754 float word `C0C80000h` |
| `800000 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `0h` | `480000h` | `181h` | Cleave at Bit 23: mantissa `480000h` in Y, upper 9 bits `181h` in X |
| `100 [↱] [÷R]` | `0h` | `480000h` | `81h` | `1h` | Cleave at Bit 8: Sign `1h` in X, Exponent `81h` in Y, Mantissa in Z |
| `[↰] [BASE] [DEC]` | 0 | 4718592 | 129 | 1 | Switch to Decimal: $S = 1$, $E = 129$, $M = 4,718,592$ |
| `[x⇄y] 127 [-]` | 4718592 | 4718592 | 1 | 2 | Subtract bias $127$ to reveal true binary exponent $e = 2$ |

Similarly, for the upper 32-bit word `0xC02AC000` of $-13.375_{10}$ (`0xC02AC00000000000`, `binary64`) in `[HEX]` mode, chaining `C02AC000 [ENTER] 100000 [↱] [÷R] 800 [↱] [÷R]` cleaves at $2^{20} = \text{100000h}$ and $2^{11} = \text{800h}$ to leave Sign $S = \mathbf{1}$ in $X$, Biased Exponent $E = \mathbf{\text{402h}}$ ($1026_{10}$, $e = 1026 - 1023 = \mathbf{3}$) in $Y$, and significand `AC000h` ($704,512 / 2^{20} = 0.671875$) in $Z$ for $(-1)^1 \times 2^3 \times 1.671875 = \mathbf{-13.375}$.

### 10.5.6 Combinatorics (PROB) & Birthday Paradox Collision Probability

In `[DEC]` mode, the `[↱] [PROB]` menu (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[eˣ]`) evaluates discrete state spaces on the stack. For a 12-drive array selecting $5$ drives for an unordered RAID group ($C(12, 5)$) versus an ordered failover chain ($P(12, 5)$), `12 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r]` counts $\mathbf{792}$ subsets, while `12 [ENTER] 5 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r]` spans $\mathbf{95,040}$ sequences:

* **4-Stage Non-Repeating Hex Shift Register ($P(16, 4)$):** Assigning an ordered 4-nibble sequence without repetition from $16$ hexadecimal digits via `16 [ENTER] 4 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r]` yields `43,680` distinct register states.
* **7-Router Full-Mesh Point-to-Point Links ($C(7, 2)$):** Wiring every unordered pair of routers across a 7-node network via `7 [ENTER] 2 [↱] [PROB] [Cn,r]` requires `21` cables.
* **15-Packet Priority Queue Permutations ($15!$):** Ordering an entire 15-packet queue via `15 [↱] [PROB] [↰] [x!]` spans `1,307,674,368,000` schedules ($12! = 479,001,600$ for $12$ items).

Evaluating Richard von Mises's Birthday Collision probability $1 - P(365, k)/365^k$ across $N = 365$ days for $k = 23$ people ($\binom{23}{2} = 253\text{ pairs}$) via `365 [ENTER] 23 [↱] [PROB] [Pn,r]` gives $4.220082 \times 10^{58}$ collision-free assignments; dividing by `365 [ENTER] 23 [yˣ] [÷]` yields $P_{\text{unique}} = \mathbf{0.492703}$, and `1 [x⇄y] [-]` confirms a shared-birthday probability of $\mathbf{0.507297}$ ($50.73\%$).

# Chapter 11: Compound Interest, Amortization & the Time Value of Money

## 11.1 Fibonacci's Merchants, Percentage Asymmetry & The Rule of 72

In 1202, Leonardo Pisano, known to posterity as Fibonacci, returned to Pisa from the commercial ports of Bugia (in modern-day Algeria), Alexandria, and Constantinople. His father, Guglielmo Bonacci, had served as a customs official representing Pisan traders across North Africa, and young Leonardo had grown up watching Arab and North African mathematicians calculate with the nine Hindu-Arabic numerals (`1` through `9`) and the symbol `zephirum` (`0`), while European counting houses were still struggling to multiply Roman numerals (`MCCIV`) on counting boards.

When Fibonacci completed his treatise *Liber Abaci* (*The Book of Calculation*) in 1202, popular history remembered the work chiefly for its exercise on breeding rabbits. In fact, that rabbit problem occupied barely half a page. Fibonacci filled the longest, most ambitious chapters of *Liber Abaci* with the real mathematical problem that kept twelfth-century Venetian, Genovese, and Pisan sea captains awake at night: comparing the worth of a gold bezant in hand today against a stream of payments arriving across different years in the future.

Four centuries later, after Simon Stevin printed the first public compound-interest tables in Leiden (*Tafelen van Interest*, 1582), English mathematician Richard Witt published *Arithmeticall Questions, Touching the Buying or Exchange of Annuities* in 1613 London, just one year before John Napier unveiled his logarithms in Edinburgh. Witt demonstrated to London merchants, landlords, and actuaries that time acts as a geometric operator on capital: every period that a principal $PV$ is invested at periodic rate $i$, it scales by the growth factor $(1 + i)$. Conversely, every period one must wait to receive a promised future sum $FV$, its present value is discounted through division by $(1 + i)$.

Across personal savings, amortizing residential mortgages, fixed-income securities, and corporate capital budgeting, compound growth and present-value discounting translate cash flows occurring at different dates into a single common measure of value.

### 11.1.1 Multiplicative Asymmetry in Percentage Gains and Losses

Even over a two-period horizon, percentage changes exhibit a fundamental asymmetry between gains and losses. When a portfolio of initial value $V_0$ suffers a fractional drawdown of $\delta$ during an autumn sell-off, and then rallies by an equal fractional gain of $+\delta$ the following spring, linear intuition—trained on symmetric addition and subtraction ($-\delta + \delta = 0$)—expects the portfolio to return to its starting balance $V_0$.

Tracing the capital across the two periods reveals the multiplicative asymmetry. Losing a fraction $\delta$ first reduces the initial capital $V_0$ to a diminished base of $V_1 = V_0(1 - \delta)$; for a $20\%$ drop on $\$100.00$, the capital shrinks to $\$80.00$. When the market subsequently rebounds by $+\delta$, that percentage gain acts on the shrunken base $V_1$ rather than on $V_0$, bringing the terminal value to $V_2 = V_1(1 + \delta) = V_0(1 - \delta)(1 + \delta)$. On the $\$80.00$ base, a $+20\%$ gain adds only $+\$16.00$ and ends at $\$96.00$, so the portfolio remains down by $-4.0\%$. More dramatically, when an asset loses half its value ($\delta = 50\%$), a subsequent $+50\%$ gain restores only three-quarters of the initial principal; full recovery to $V_0$ requires solving $V_0(1 - \delta)(1 + g) = V_0$, which demands a hyperbolic recovery gain of $g = \frac{\delta}{1 - \delta}$ (or $+100\%$ after a $50\%$ loss, and $+25\%$ after a $20\%$ loss).

Equal percentage losses and gains never cancel out because percentages compose multiplicatively rather than additively. By the algebraic identity for the difference of two squares, a fractional drop $-\delta$ followed by an equal fractional gain $+\delta$ produces:

$$(1 - \delta)(1 + \delta) = 1 - \delta^2 < 1$$

Whenever $\delta > 0$, the product $(1 - \delta)(1 + \delta)$ falls short of unity by the quadratic volatility drag $\delta^2$ (for $\delta = 0.20$, the drag is $\delta^2 = 0.04 = 4\%$).

That same multiplicative structure governs successive chain markdowns and commercial gross-margin pricing. When a merchant applies a primary fractional markdown $d_1$ followed by an additional promotional discount $d_2$ at checkout, the two concessions do not sum to $d_1 + d_2$. Instead, the net retention factor is the product $(1 - d_1)(1 - d_2)$, so the effective combined discount is $d_{\text{eff}} = 1 - (1 - d_1)(1 - d_2) = d_1 + d_2 - d_1 d_2$. A $50\%$ clearance markdown followed by an extra $40\%$ off retains $0.50 \times 0.60 = 0.30$ of list price, an effective discount of $70\%$ rather than $90\%$.

Similarly, in commercial accounting, a markup rate $r$ is measured as a fraction of unit landed cost $C$ to produce a selling price of $P_{\text{markup}} = C(1 + r)$, whereas a gross margin requirement $m$ specifies the fraction of the final selling price $P$ retained as gross profit, $(P - C)/P = m$. Applying a cost markup of $r = m$ realizes a gross margin of only $\frac{m}{1 + m}$. To achieve a true target gross margin $m$, the unit cost $C$ must represent the complement $(1 - m)$ of the selling price:

$$P_{\text{margin}} = \frac{C}{1 - m}$$

### 11.1.2 Base-Preserving Percentages and the Logarithmic Rule of 72

Everyday percentage calculations frequently go astray because every percentage only has meaning relative to its reference base.

In the 1970s, Hewlett-Packard's RPN calculator architects and UC Berkeley numerical analyst William M. Kahan, the chief architect of the IEEE-754 floating-point standard and financial solver algorithms *([Kahan, 1979](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-kahan1979))*, examined why conventional pocket calculators make percentage math so error-prone. On an algebraic calculator, computing a tax or discount rate $r\%$ on an invoice base $B$ via `B × r %` overwrites the display with the adjustment $B \cdot r / 100$ and destroys the original base $B$, so the operator must re-enter the base from scratch to obtain the net total.

Hewlett-Packard's architects and Kahan recognized that in an inside-out stack architecture, the percentage operator must be a two-register state transformation $(Y, X) \mapsto (Y, Y \cdot X / 100)$ that preserves the reference base in Register $Y$. On the SC-32, `[↱] [%]` (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[COS]`) and `[↱] [%CHG]` (Right Shift `[↱]` above `[TAN]`) enforce this base-preserving invariant. Staging the base amount in Register $Y$ and the percentage rate in Register $X$ lets `[↱] [%]` place the exact currency adjustment in Register $X$ while holding the original base untouched in Register $Y$, ready for `[+]` to add a tax or `[-]` to deduct a markdown in a single keystroke.

When a periodic growth rate $r\%$ compounds across $N$ consecutive periods, each period multiplies the balance by $(1 + r/100)$ and compounds additive rates into exponential growth:

$$FV = PV \left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^N$$

To find the number of periods $N$ required for compound growth at rate $r\%$ to double an initial principal ($FV / PV = 2$), take the natural logarithm of both sides:

$$\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right)^N = 2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad N \ln\!\left(1 + \frac{r}{100}\right) = \ln 2 \approx 0.693147$$

For moderate rates ($r \le 12\%$), the Mercator-Taylor expansion $\ln(1 + u) = u - \frac{1}{2}u^2 + \cdots$ with $u = r/100$ gives $N \approx \frac{69.31}{r}\left(1 + \frac{r}{200}\right)$. Franciscan friar Luca Pacioli, who first printed the rule in his monumental *Summa de arithmetica* (Venice, 1494), and Renaissance merchants across Venice and Florence adjusted the numerator from $69.3$ to $72$ (matching the exact discrete-compounding curvature around $r \approx 8\%$) because $72$ is evenly divisible by $1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9,$ and $12$ to establish the Rule of 72:

$$\text{Doubling Time (Years)} \approx \frac{72}{\text{Annual Interest Rate } r\%}$$

At $6\%$ annual return, capital doubles in approximately $72 / 6 = 12\text{ years}$; at $8\%$, in $72 / 8 = 9\text{ years}$; at $9\%$, in $72 / 9 = 8\text{ years}$. Conversely, when price inflation runs at an annual rate $\pi$ over $N$ years, the real purchasing power of uninvested cash decays exponentially according to $PV_{\text{real}} = FV \cdot (1 + \pi)^{-N}$ and cuts purchasing power in half every $72 / (100\pi)$ years.

## 11.2 The Five-Variable Balance Law and Mortgage Amortization

### 11.2.1 Deriving the Five-Variable TVM Balance Equation

In practice, financial contracts rarely involve a single lump sum left untouched for decades. Instead, three distinct cash components interact across $N$ compounding periods at periodic interest rate $i$: the present value $PV$ exchanged at time $t = 0$ (such as loan principal disbursed at closing or an opening investment balance), the uniform periodic payment stream $PMT$ transferred at each period $k = 1, 2, \dots, N$ (such as a periodic loan installment, lease payment, or sinking-fund contribution), and the terminal future value $FV$ remaining at the end of period $N$ ($0$ for a fully amortizing loan, a contractual balloon payoff, or an accumulated savings target). All five variables—$N, i, PV, PMT,$ and $FV$—are unified by Francis Baily's (1808) and Augustus De Morgan's (1838) principle of actuarial equivalence, which discounts every cash flow to a common reference epoch.

Taking the present epoch ($t = 0$) as the valuation fulcrum, each periodic payment $PMT$ occurring at period $k$ is discounted to $t = 0$ through multiplication by $(1 + i)^{-k}$, and the terminal balance $FV$ at period $N$ is discounted by $(1 + i)^{-N}$:

$$PV + \frac{PMT}{(1+i)^1} + \frac{PMT}{(1+i)^2} + \cdots + \frac{PMT}{(1+i)^N} + \frac{FV}{(1+i)^N} = 0$$

The central summation of $N$ discounted payments is a finite geometric series with common ratio $q = (1 + i)^{-1}$. Applying Euclid's closed-form summation identity collapses those $N$ terms into the standard actuarial Annuity Present-Value Factor ($a_{\overline{N}|i}$):

$$\sum_{k=1}^{N} (1 + i)^{-k} = \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} = a_{\overline{N}|i}$$

Substituting $a_{\overline{N}|i}$ yields the Master Five-Variable Time Value of Money (`TVM`) Equation:

$$PV + PMT \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i} \right] + FV (1 + i)^{-N} = 0$$

Payment timing within each period modifies the annuity factor. In an Ordinary Annuity (`END` mode), standard for residential mortgages, term loans, and coupon bonds, each payment $PMT$ occurs at the end of its compounding period after one interval of interest has accrued. In an Annuity Due (`BEG` mode), standard for real-estate leases, equipment rentals, and insurance premiums, each payment occurs at the beginning of the period, so it compounds for one extra interval and multiplies the $PMT$ bracket by $(1 + i)$.

### 11.2.2 Cash-Flow Conservation and the Sign Convention

The right-hand side of the Master TVM Equation equals zero because every financial contract conserves discounted value across time. Financial mathematics models an individual wallet or corporate treasury as a thermodynamic control volume across time, governed by a strict directional sign convention. Cash inflows entering the operator's hands, such as loan proceeds received at closing, coupon checks collected, or maturity redemptions paid out, carry a positive sign ($+$). Cash outflows leaving the operator's hands, such as periodic loan repayments, savings deposits transferred into an external account, or the purchase price paid to acquire a security, carry a negative sign ($-$).

When all inflows and outflows along the timeline are discounted to $t = 0$ at periodic rate $i$, their algebraic sum vanishes. This sign discipline makes the direction of every transaction unambiguous: when a borrower receives loan proceeds $PV > 0$ at $t = 0$, the $N$ periodic repayments must carry the opposite sign ($PMT < 0$) to reduce the remaining debt to $FV = 0$.

![Time Value of Money (TVM) cash-flow sign conservation timeline and 30-year mortgage principal-versus-interest amortization crossover.](../assets/manuals/sc32_concept_tvm_cashflow.png)

### 11.2.3 Principal-Interest Decomposition and Amortization Crossover

For a fully amortizing level-payment loan of principal $PV > 0$ repaid across $N$ periods (`FV = 0`) at periodic interest rate $i$, solving the Master TVM Equation fixes the constant periodic payment magnitude $|PMT|$:

$$|PMT| = PV \left[ \frac{i}{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}} \right]$$

Although the total check $|PMT|$ remains constant at every period $k = 1, 2, \dots, N$, its internal allocation between interest charge $I_k$ and principal reduction $P_k$ shifts exponentially over the life of the contract. At the end of period $k - 1$, the remaining loan balance $B_{k-1}$ equals the present value of the $N - k + 1$ payments still remaining:

$$B_{k-1} = |PMT| \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-(N - k + 1)}}{i} \right]$$

During period $k$, the lender first assesses periodic interest $I_k = i \cdot B_{k-1}$ on that outstanding balance, and only the residual portion $P_k = |PMT| - I_k$ reduces the principal:

$$I_k = |PMT| \left[ 1 - (1 + i)^{-(N - k + 1)} \right], \qquad P_k = |PMT| (1 + i)^{-(N - k + 1)}$$

These two identities govern the structural dynamics of every amortizing loan. Because $P_{k+1} / P_k = 1 + i$, the principal portion of each payment follows a geometric progression that grows exponentially at rate $i$ from the first period to the last. On long-duration loans where $N \cdot i \gg 1$, the factor $(1 + i)^{-N}$ is small, so $I_1$ consumes the overwhelming majority of the opening payments while $P_1$ retires only a small fraction of principal. The amortization crossover period $k_{\text{cross}}$ at which principal reduction $P_k$ finally overtakes interest $I_k$ occurs when $P_k = \frac{1}{2}|PMT|$, which simplifies directly to $(1 + i)^{N - k + 1} = 2$. Taking logarithms reveals that the crossover point depends only on $N$ and $i$, completely independent of the loan size $PV$:

$$k_{\text{cross}} = N + 1 - \frac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + i)}$$

Thus, the amortization crossover always occurs exactly one Rule-of-72 doubling time prior to maturity. Furthermore, because early principal reduction $P_k$ is small, sending an unscheduled periodic principal curtailment $\Delta P$ on top of $|PMT|$ accelerates the payoff horizon from $N$ down to $N^*$, derived in closed form by inverting the annuity factor:

$$N^* = -\frac{\ln\!\left(1 - \frac{i \cdot PV}{|PMT| + \Delta P}\right)}{\ln(1 + i)}$$

Each extra dollar directed to principal in early periods bypasses all compound interest that would otherwise accrue on that dollar across the remaining $N - k$ periods of the schedule.

## 11.3 Valuing Future Cash Streams: Bond Pricing, Net Present Value & Internal Rate of Return

### 11.3.1 Coupon Discounting, Inverse Yield Dynamics, and Macaulay Duration

A fixed-rate bond is a standardized loan contract in which an issuer promises to pay a sequence of periodic coupon inflows $PMT = +C$ across $N$ compounding periods together with a par redemption inflow $FV = +M$ at maturity. When the market requires a periodic yield to maturity $y$ on securities of comparable credit risk, the fair purchase price $P$ (entered as an acquisition outflow $PV = -P$) is the sum of the discounted coupons and discounted par redemption:

$$P(y) = C \left[ \frac{1 - (1 + y)^{-N}}{y} \right] + M (1 + y)^{-N}$$

Because the contractual cash promises $C$ and $M$ are fixed at issuance, the market price $P(y)$ moves inversely to the prevailing yield $y$. When the market yield $y$ equals the coupon rate $c = C / M$, the bond trades at par ($P = M$); when prevailing yields rise above the coupon rate ($y > c$), the bond must trade at a discount ($P < M$) so that the capital gain $M - P$ at maturity compensates the buyer for the below-market coupons; when yields fall below the coupon rate ($y < c$), the bond trades at a premium ($P > M$).

In 1938, economist Frederick Macaulay introduced a closed-form measure of a bond's effective maturity and interest-rate sensitivity by treating the discounted cash flows $w_t = C_t (1 + y)^{-t}$ at epochs $t = 1, 2, \dots, N$ as point masses distributed along a timeline. The center-of-mass fulcrum where that timeline balances—identical in form to Archimedes' weighted centroid $\bar{t} = \frac{\sum t w_t}{\sum w_t}$—is Macaulay Duration ($D$). Differentiating $P(y)$ with respect to $y$ and dividing $D$ by $(1 + y)$ yields Modified Duration ($D^*$), the first-order elasticity linking percentage price changes to yield shifts $\Delta y$:

$$D = \frac{1}{P} \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{t \cdot C_t}{(1 + y)^t}, \qquad \frac{\Delta P}{P} \approx -D^* \cdot \Delta y = -\frac{D}{1 + y} \cdot \Delta y$$

This duration lever explains why short-dated notes with small $D^*$ exhibit minimal price volatility when central-bank rates move, whereas long-dated bonds—whose cash-flow centroid sits far out along the time axis—experience large percentage price swings for every $1\%$ shift in yield.

### 11.3.2 Net Present Value (`NPV`) as a Horner Polynomial and `IRR` Root-Finding

Unlike level-coupon bonds, capital projects, industrial plants, and operating businesses generate uneven cash flows $C_1, C_2, \dots, C_N$ across successive years. Discounting each cash flow at the firm's periodic cost of capital $r$ defines the present value of the stream (and, after subtracting the initial outlay $|C_0|$, the Net Present Value):

$$\text{PV}(r) = \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}, \qquad \text{NPV}(r) = C_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{N} \frac{C_t}{(1 + r)^t}$$

Letting $x = 1 + r$ represent the gross periodic discount factor, the discounted sum is a degree-$N$ polynomial in the reciprocal factor $u = 1/x$, which folds from the terminal horizon $t = N$ backward to $t = 0$ via Horner's nested recurrence:

$$\text{NPV}(x) = C_0 + \left(\cdots\left(\left(C_N \div x + C_{N-1}\right) \div x + C_{N-2}\right) \div x + \cdots + C_1\right) \div x$$

This nested polynomial representation directly governs the inverse valuation problem: given an initial investment outlay $C_0 < 0$ followed by future cash flows $C_1, \dots, C_N$, the Internal Rate of Return (`IRR`) is the critical discount rate $r^*$ at which the Net Present Value vanishes, $\text{NPV}(r^*) = 0$.

Determining `IRR`—or solving the Master TVM Equation for an unknown periodic rate `I%` (`[I%YR]` on `[LFU1]`)—requires finding the root of a degree-$N$ polynomial. As Niels Henrik Abel and Évariste Galois proved in the nineteenth century, no closed-form radical formula exists for general polynomial equations of degree $N \ge 5$. Moreover, as William Kahan demonstrated in his 1979 analysis of financial calculators, direct evaluation of $\frac{1 - (1 + i)^{-N}}{i}$ suffers catastrophic cancellation when $i \to 0$, requiring evaluation through $\ln(1 + i)$ and $\exp(x) - 1$ primitives during iterative root-finding:

$$a_{\overline{N}|i} = \frac{1 - \exp\!\left(-N \ln(1 + i)\right)}{i}$$

Two structural properties govern numerical root-finding on discounted cash-flow polynomials. First, `NPV` and `IRR` can rank mutually exclusive projects differently when their scales or cash-flow timings diverge: `IRR` implicitly assumes intermediate cash inflows can be reinvested at the internal rate $r^*$ itself, whereas `NPV` discounts every cash flow at the external opportunity cost of capital $r$.

Second, by René Descartes's 1637 Rule of Signs, a conventional investment whose cash-flow sequence changes sign only once ($C_0 < 0$ followed by $C_t \ge 0$) possesses a unique positive root $x^* = 1 + r^*$. By contrast, a project with a large terminal decommissioning or reclamation outflow ($-, +, +, -$) changes sign twice and can exhibit two distinct internal rates of return. To handle both regimes cleanly, the SC-32 combines Horner stack evaluation with Richard Brent's `[↱] [SOLVE]` root-finder and William Kahan's financial convergence safeguards *([Kahan, 1979](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-kahan1979); [Brent, 1973](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-brent1973))* across `N`, `I%`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`, and `END`/`BEG`.

## 11.4 Percentages, Mortgage Amortization & Discounted Cash Flows

Because a unit of capital today compounds at periodic rate $i$ into $(1 + i)^N$ units $N$ periods hence, every commercial invoice, amortizing loan, bond, or capital budget is governed by discounted cash-flow conservation. On the StackCalc SC-32, financial computation relies on a two-register discipline: Register `Y` holds the baseline principal or subtotal untouched while Register `X` evaluates `[↱] [%]` or `[↱] [%CHG]`, and the five-variable `[↰] [TVM]` softkey bar (`[N]`, `[I%YR]`, `[PV]`, `[PMT]`, `[FV]`) reads known inputs from and writes solved roots directly to Register `X` without disturbing the upper stack.

Pressing `[↰] [TVM]` (Left Shift `[↰]` above `[x∥y]`) maps the five financial variables plus `END/BEG` across the six top softkeys (`[LFU0]`–`[LFU5]`), where two operational invariants govern every entry. Under the wallet reference frame, cash flowing into your pocket is entered as positive (`+`), whereas cash flowing out of your pocket is negated with `[+/-]` (`-`). To solve for an unknown quantity from four known parameters, keying a number and tapping a softkey stores that parameter from Register `X`, while tapping a fifth softkey without prior numeric entry solves for that unknown variable.

![The SC-32 transflective display executing multi-variable financial calculations with continuous stack preservation.](../assets/manuals/screenshots/sc32_tvm_mortgage.png)

### 11.4.1 Base-Preserving Percentages (`%`), Chain Discounts & Gross Margin Pricing

To format currency outputs rounded to cents while retaining full 64-bit internal precision, set the display mode to two decimal places (`[FIX] 2`) via `[↰] [DISP]` $\to$ `[FIX]` $\to$ `2` *([HP, 1982](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-hp15c1982))*. On the StackCalc SC-32, the Percentage Function (`[↱] [%]`) adheres strictly to William Kahan's non-destructive specification *([Kahan, 1979](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-kahan1979))*:

$$\text{Calculation: } \quad X \leftarrow \frac{Y \times X}{100}, \quad Y \leftarrow Y \text{ (Preserved)}, \quad \text{Lift} \leftarrow \text{TRUE}$$

Because `[↱] [%]` leaves your original base amount intact in Register $Y$ while placing the computed dollar adjustment directly beneath it in Register $X$ (with Registers $Z$ and $T$ at zero), everyday commercial calculations flow in two natural moves:
* **Consulting Invoice Tax (`$150.00 + 8.25%`):** To add $8.25\%$ sales tax to a $\$150.00$ invoice, keying `150 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` places the $\$12.38$ tax in Register $X$ while holding $\$150.00$ in Register $Y$, so pressing `[+]` completes the $\$162.38$ total in one stroke. Likewise, running `100 [ENTER] 8 [↱] [%]` on a $\$100.00$ baseline leaves the exact dollar adjustment (`8`) in Register $X$ while freezing $100.00$ in Register $Y$.
* **Enterprise Server Purchase Order (`$18,450.00 + 8.25%`):** On an enterprise server order subtotaling $\$18,450.00$ with $8.25\%$ state sales tax (`[FIX] 2`), keying `18450 [ENTER] 8.25 [↱] [%]` stages $\$18,450.00$ in Register $Y$, computes the $\$1,522.13$ sales tax in Register $X$, and sums the two registers to `$19,972.13` without retyping the base.
* **Single Volume Discount (`$85,000.00 - 17.5%`):** On an $\$85,000.00$ software license carrying a $17.5\%$ volume discount, `85000 [ENTER] 17.5 [↱] [%]` places the $\$14,875.00$ concession in Register $X$ directly beneath the $\$85,000.00$ list price in Register $Y$, so subtracting settles the net invoice payable at `$70,125.00`.
* **Stacked Chain Markdowns (`$280.00 - 30% - 15%`):** When a $30\%$ seasonal sale is followed by an extra $15\%$ VIP coupon on a $\$280.00$ field jacket, evaluating `280 [ENTER] 30 [↱] [%]` and subtracting the initial $\$84.00$ markdown leaves the intermediate $\$196.00$ sale price in Register $X$; applying the second $15\%$ discount ($\$29.40$) via `15 [↱] [%] [-]` then lands at $\$166.60$, an effective $40.5\%$ reduction rather than $45\%$.
* **Shared vs. Itemized Bill Splitting:** When $8$ diners split a $\$480.00$ restaurant tab where $3$ guests shared $\$96.00$ of wine while all $8$ split the food equally, deducting the wine tab via `480 [ENTER] 96 [-]` isolates the $\$384.00$ food subtotal and divides by $8$ to establish the $\$48.00$ per-person food share in Register $X$; chaining `96 [ENTER] 3 [÷]` then stages the $\$32.00$ per-drinker wine share in Register $X$ beneath $\$48.00$ in $Y$ and adds them to finish the wine-drinker total ($\$80.00$).

By contrast, comparing the Markup Trap against true Gross Margin Pricing on a product with landed cost $C = \$60.00$ and target $40.0\%$ gross margin activates all four stack registers so you can hold the flawed markup price in the upper registers while computing the true margin price below: adding a $40\%$ markup onto $\$60.00$ (`60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%] [+]` $\rightarrow$ `$84.00`) yields only $\$24 / \$84 = 28.57\%$ margin, whereas dividing cost by the margin complement $\text{Price} = \frac{\text{Cost}}{1 - \text{Margin}}$ via `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER] 0.40 [-] [÷]` resolves the true retail price `$100.00`:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| `60 [ENTER] 40 [↱] [%]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 60.00 | 24.00 | 40% markup on \$60.00 cost: \$24.00 |
| `[+]` | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 84.00 | Flawed markup price: \$84.00 (28.57% margin) |
| `60 [ENTER] 1 [ENTER]` | 84.00 | 60.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | True margin pricing: stage cost \$60 in $Z$ and 1.00 in $Y$ |
| `.40 [-]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 60.00 | 0.60 | 1 - 0.40 = 0.60 margin complement; \$60.00 drops to $Y$ |
| `[÷]` | 84.00 | 84.00 | 84.00 | 100.00 | True gross margin retail price: \$100.00 |

### 11.4.2 Percent Change (`%CHG`), Cross-Metric Elasticity, CAGR & Inflation

The Percent Change Function (`[↱] [%CHG]`) is executed via Right Shift `[↱]` followed by `[%CHG]` using the chronological order Old Value `[ENTER]` New Value `[↱] [%CHG]`, preserving the Old Value in Register $Y$ and the New Value in `LASTX`.

In a quarterly SaaS operating review where Annual Recurring Revenue (`ARR`) grew from $\$12.0\text{M}$ to $\$15.6\text{M}$, `12 [ENTER] 15.6 [↱] [%CHG]` returns $+30.00\%$. Over the same period, Customer Acquisition Cost (`CAC`) expanded from $\$2.4\text{M}$ to $\$2.88\text{M}$, where `2.4 [ENTER] 2.88 [↱] [%CHG]` returns $+20.00\%$. Dropping the old baseline out of the way via `[x⇄y] [R↓]` aligns `ARR` growth in Register $Y$ ($30.00$) and `CAC` growth in Register $X$ ($20.00$) side-by-side on the stack. Pressing `[-]` then gives the `+10.00%` growth spread, while `30 [ENTER] 20 [÷]` delivers the `1.5` growth elasticity multiplier:

| Keystroke | Register T | Register Z | Register Y | Register X | What Happens on the Stack |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |

### 11.4.3 The Five-Variable `TVM` Engine: Mortgages, Amortization & Balloon Notes

The onboard Five-Variable Time Value of Money (`[↰] [TVM]`) Engine is accessed via Left Shift `[↰]` above `[x∥y]` (Row 7, Column 3):

| **$I\%$** | `[I%YR]` (`[LFU1]`) | Periodic interest rate per compounding period ($i\%$) | Percent per period (e.g. `6.5` for 6.5%/yr or `6.75/12 = 0.5625` for monthly) |

Four hardware state conventions govern the `[↰] [TVM]` softkey interface:
1. **Store versus Solve Dispatch:** Tapping any `[↰] [TVM]` softkey immediately after numeric entry or an arithmetic operation stores Register $X$ into that financial register; tapping a softkey immediately after another `[↰] [TVM]` softkey solves for that unknown variable into Register $X$.
2. **Periodic Interest Rate Scaling:** Softkey `[I%YR]` (`[LFU1]`) stores the periodic interest rate $i\%$ per compounding interval. For a monthly contract quoted at nominal annual rate $\text{APR}$, divide by $12$ (`6.75 [ENTER] 12 [÷]` $\to 0.5625\%$) before storing.
3. **Payment Timing Mode (`END/BEG`):** Softkey `[LFU5]` toggles between Ordinary Annuity (`END`, end-of-period cash flows) and Annuity Due (`BEG`, beginning-of-period cash flows).
4. **Register Persistence Across Scenarios:** All five `[↰] [TVM]` registers retain their stored parameters across calculations for sensitivity analysis; explicitly zero any unused variable (such as `0 [FV]` or `[↰] [CLEAR]` $\to$ `[CLVARS]` on `[LFU1]`) before starting an unrelated contract.

Applying this five-variable sequence to a 30-year fixed residential mortgage of $PV = +\$350,000.00$ at $6.75\%$ APR establishes the monthly payment and lifetime interest burden:
1. **Total Periods (`N = 360`):** Thirty years of monthly payments span $30 \times 12 = 360$ compounding periods $\to$ `360 [N]`.
2. **Monthly Periodic Rate (`I% = 6.75 / 12 = 0.5625`):** Divide the $6.75\%$ annual rate by $12$ months to get $0.5625\%$ per month $\to$ `.5625 [I%YR]`.
3. **Present Value Loan Inflow (`PV = +350000`):** At closing, the lender wires $+\$350,000.00$ into your transaction $\to$ `350000 [PV]`.
4. **Target Future Payoff Balance (`FV = 0`):** A fully amortizing mortgage pays the balance down to zero at Month 360 $\to$ `0 [FV]`.
5. **Solve for the Unknown Monthly Outflow (`PMT`):** With four variables stored, tap `[PMT]` without typing a number to solve for the monthly check ($-\$2,270.09$):

# Chapter 12: Cartesian Coordinates, Pixel Rasterization & Visual Analysis

## 12.1 René Descartes's Coordinate Plane and the Geometry of Functions

### 12.1.1 Algebraic Equations as Geometric Loci

During his years as a boarding student at the College of La Flèche in Anjou, René Descartes was granted an unusual privilege by the rector, Father Charlet: while his classmates rose at five o'clock every morning to recite Latin prayers in unheated stone halls, young René was allowed to remain warm under his blankets until late morning, thinking quietly with his eyes open.

Descartes kept that habit of morning meditation for the rest of his life. Observing the orthogonal grid of ceiling tiles and wall joints in his room—and investigating Pappus of Alexandria's classical locus problem—Descartes considered how to specify the exact position of a moving point on a flat plane at any instant, and how to describe the path it traced.

He realized that if he measured the perpendicular distance $x$ from a horizontal reference axis and the perpendicular distance $y$ from a second reference axis, every position on the plane corresponded to a unique pair of numbers $(x, y)$. If the point moved along a straight diagonal line or a smooth circular arc, its two distances $x$ and $y$ obeyed a strict algebraic equation; conversely, *any* algebraic equation connecting $x$ and $y$ traced a visible geometric curve across the plane.

When Descartes published this discovery in 1637 as *La Géométrie* *([Descartes, 1637](sc32/appendix-e-annotated-bibliography.md#cite-descartes1637))*, an appendix to his *Discourse on the Method*, he ended a two-thousand-year separation that had divided mathematical thought since antiquity. Ancient Greek geometry, as practiced by Euclid, Archimedes, and Apollonius, was rich in visual intuition with circles, triangles, parabolas, and tangent lines drawn by straightedge and compass, yet it possessed almost no symbolic algebra, so proving a new theorem required inventing a custom geometric construction from scratch. Conversely, medieval and Renaissance algebra, developed by al-Khwarizmi, Tartaglia, Cardano, and Viète, provided a symbolic calculus for balancing unknowns ($x^2, x^3$), yet an equation sat on the page as a dry string of characters with no visual shape.

Descartes proved that algebra and geometry are two languages describing one underlying reality. John Stuart Mill later called analytic geometry *"the greatest single step ever made in the progress of the exact sciences,"* because it gave equations eyes and gave geometric shapes formulas.

### 12.1.2 Reading the Anatomy of a Curve: Roots, Peaks, Valleys & Inflection Points

Once an algebraic formula $y = f(x)$ is translated into a Cartesian curve across a horizontal $x$-axis (domain) and a vertical $y$-axis (range), defined on the SC-32 via the `[↱] [EQN]` editor, every analytical feature from Algebra II, Precalculus, and introductory calculus corresponds to a distinct geometric contour along the curve.

Hunting for the roots or zeros of a polynomial or transcendental equation means searching for values of $x$ where $f(x) = 0$. On a Cartesian graph, a root is a shoreline where the terrain crosses sea level ($y = 0$) and switches from negative elevation ($y < 0$, underwater) to positive elevation ($y > 0$, dry land). Along a smooth curve, the first derivative $f'(x)$ measures the instantaneous slope: as an observer climbs a hill, the slope is positive ($f'(x) > 0$), and on the descent down the far side, the slope is negative ($f'(x) < 0$). At the exact summit of a smooth hill (*local maximum*) or the bottom of a smooth valley (*local minimum*), the tangent line is momentarily flat and horizontal ($f'(x) = 0$).

An *inflection point* marks a reversal in the sign of curvature along a smooth trajectory, such as an S-shaped highway transition modeled by a general cubic polynomial:

$$y(x) = a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d, \qquad y''(x) = 6ax + 2b$$

Wherever the second derivative is negative ($y''(x) < 0$), the tangent slope decreases with $x$ and the curve bends downward (*concave down*); wherever the second derivative is positive ($y''(x) > 0$), the tangent slope increases with $x$ and the curve bends upward (*concave up*). At the unique abscissa $x_{\text{infl}} = -\frac{b}{3a}$ where $y''(x_{\text{infl}}) = 0$, the curvature passes through zero as the trajectory reverses its direction of bend, which forms the exact geometric point of symmetry between the cubic's local peak and local valley.

Vertical and horizontal asymptotes bound the extreme behavior of rational and exponential functions. When a rational denominator approaches zero, such as the thin-lens magnification formula $f(x) = \frac{1}{x - 2}$ as an object crosses the focal point $x = 2$, the curve diverges toward $-\infty$ on the left and plunges from $+\infty$ on the right along a *vertical asymptote*. Conversely, when a skydiver falls under gravity $g$ and quadratic air drag ($v(t) = v_{\text{term}}\tanh(gt/v_{\text{term}})$), or when an uncharged capacitor charges through a resistor toward a supply voltage $V_{\max}$ with RC time constant $\tau$:

$$V(t) = V_{\max}\!\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$$

upward air resistance or capacitor back-voltage gradually balances the driving force, and the curve approaches a flat horizontal ceiling—a *horizontal asymptote* at $v = v_{\text{term}}$ or $V = V_{\max}$ as $t \to \infty$.
