## C.2 Architectural Refinements, Dynamic LFU Menus & Complete HP-32SII / HP-15C / HP-12C Comparison

The SC-32 keypad layout follows the Dvorak Principle applied to calculators: whereas computer terminals and menu-driven graphing calculators place common operations inside nested menu trees, routine scientific and engineering calculations on a handheld instrument should execute from direct tactile keystrokes.

### C.2.1 The Corvallis HP-32SII Structural Foundation

The 1991 HP-32SII Pioneer provides an ergonomic and symbolic baseline for a portrait RPN scientific instrument. Its one-handed geometry keeps the digit pad, `[ENTER]`, and arithmetic column inside the natural sweep of a single thumb. At the same time, its 26 automatic alpha variables (`A`–`Z`) and symbolic Equation Bank (`[↱] [EQN]`) replace anonymous register numbers (`R0`–`R9`) and blind keystroke subroutines (`LBL 0..9`), while eight SI $\leftrightarrow$ Imperial unit conversions (expanded to ten on the SC-32) and native rational fractions (`[↰] [FDISP]`, `[↱] [/c]`) sit directly on the number pad.

The SC-32 preserves that 1991 Pioneer matrix while replacing its 1-line display and infix-equation mode with a 4-line stack display and pure RPN equation steps. It also integrates the analytical engines of the 1982 HP-15C Voyager (`[↱] [SOLVE]`, `[↱] [∫]`, `[↰] [CMPLX]`), a closed-form quadratic/cubic `[↱] [POLY]` engine, and the 1981 HP-12C Voyager financial functions (`[↰] [TVM]`, `[↱] [%]`, `[↱] [%CHG]`) onto shifted keys:

| Architectural Dimension | HP-12C Voyager (1981) | HP-15C Voyager (1982) | HP-32SII Pioneer (1991) | StackCalc SC-32 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Form Factor & Ergonomics** | Landscape (two-handed) | Landscape (two-handed) | Portrait (one-handed thumb arc) | Portrait 43-key Pioneer geometry (one-handed thumb arc) |
| **Display & Stack Visibility** | 1-line, 10-digit 7-seg (`X` only) | 1-line, 10-digit 7-seg (`X` only) | 1-line, 12-char dot-matrix (`X` only) | 4-line $132 \times 65$ transflective LCD ($T, Z, Y, X$ visible simultaneously) |
| **Softkey Menu Bar** | None | None | Remaps top row (`√x`..`Σ+`) with 1-line text | Dedicated 6-key Dynamic LFU Bar (`[LFU0]`–`[LFU5]`) above `√x`..`Σ+` |
| **Operational Stack Depth** | 4-level ($X, Y, Z, T$) | 4-level ($X, Y, Z, T$) | 4-level ($X, Y, Z, T$) | Selectable `[4-LVL]` (classic Corvallis), `[8-LVL]`, or `[INF]` (999-level LIFO) |
| **Storage Registers** | `R0`–`R9`, `.0`–`.9` (numbered) | `R0`–`R9`, `.0`–`.9`, `I` (numbered) | `A`–`Z` (26 named letters) + `i`, `(i)` | `A`–`Z` (26 named letters) + `i`, `(i)` across 89 indirect slots (`R1`–`R89`) |
| **Equation Bank (`EQN`)** | None (keystroke `R/S` only) | None (keystroke `LBL 0..9` only) | Algebraic infix `EQN` (`(`, `)`, `=`) | Pure RPN `[↱] [EQN]` Bank with Iverson Boolean `[x?0]`/`[x?y]` piecewise switches |
| **Root Finder & Calculus** | `IRR` / `NPV` cash-flow only | Brent `SOLVE` & Romberg `∫f(x)` via `LBL` | Brent `SOLVE` & Romberg `∫` via `EQN` | Brent `[↱] [SOLVE]` & Romberg `[↱] [∫]` via `[↱] [EQN]` + Dedicated Analytic `[↱] [POLY]` (`R34`–`R39`) |
| **Complex Numbers (`CMPLX`)** | None | Parallel complex stack via `I` / `Re⇄Im` | 4-register $(Y, X)$ & $(T, Z)$ via `CMPLX` prefix | 4-register $(Y, X)$ & $(T, Z)$ via `[↰] [CMPLX]` prefix (including complex `[x∥y]` & `[↱] [POLY]` roots) |
| **Time Value of Money (`TVM`)** | Dedicated `n`, `i`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV` keys | None | None (requires manual keystroke program) | Built-in 5-Variable `[↰] [TVM]` (`N`, `I%`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`, `END/BEG`) on `[x∥y]` |
| **Physical Unit Conversions** | None | `→H.MS`, `→RAD` only | 8 SI $\leftrightarrow$ US keys + polar/HMS/angle | 10 SI (`[↰]`) $\leftrightarrow$ US (`[↱]`) keys (adds `km` $\leftrightarrow$ `mi` on `9`) + polar/HMS/angle |
| **Exact Fractions & Number Theory** | None | None | `a b/c`, `FDISP`, `/c`; `PARTS` menu | Exact fractions (`[↰] [FDISP]`, `[↱] [/c]`), direct `[↱] [÷R]` & `[ABS]` keys (`GCD`/`LCM` in `PARTS` softkey menu) |
| **Parallel / Harmonic Operator** | None | None | None | Dedicated unshifted `[x∥y]` key ($\frac{Y \times X}{Y + X}$ for resistors, lenses, capacitors) |
| **Graphical Plotting & Exam Mode** | None | None | None | 128-column ($128 \times 52\text{ px}$) `[↱] [PLOT]` function/scatter canvas (`[x∥y]`) + proctored `[EXAM]` lockdown |

### C.2.2 Complete Key-by-Key & Menu Differences: HP-32SII vs. SC-32

Every primary key, left shift (`[↰]`, corresponding to the HP-32SII orange shift), right shift (`[↱]`, corresponding to the HP-32SII blue shift), and alpha legend on the SC-32 behaves identically to the 1991 HP-32SII except for the intentional hardware and menu additions listed below:

| Position / Menu | Key Face (SC-32 vs. HP-32SII) | Left Shift `[↰]` (SC-32 vs. HP-32SII) | Right Shift `[↱]` (SC-32 vs. HP-32SII) | Engineering Rationale for the SC-32 Design |
| :---: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **R0, C0–C5** | `[LFU0]`–`[LFU5]` *(New dedicated row)* | Dynamic LFU / Menu softkeys | Dynamic LFU / Menu softkeys | Reserves 6 dedicated physical softkeys beneath the 4-line LCD (showing 6 dynamic LFU functions in normal state and menu labels in menus) so menus never hijack `[√x]`..`[Σ+]` (`Row 1`). |
| **R3, C3** | `[+/-]` *(Same)* | `MODES` *(Adds `.` / `,` radix)* | `[ABS]` (`\|x\|`) *(HP-32SII: `(` open paren)* | Parentheses are unnecessary in RPN mode; places Absolute Value (`\|x\|`) on a direct right-shifted key while also retaining `ABS` inside the `PARTS` softkey menu. |
| **R3, C4** | `[E]` *(Same)* | `DISP` *(Same)* | `[↱] [÷R]` *(HP-32SII: `)` close paren)* | Parentheses are unnecessary in RPN mode; adds Euclidean integer division (`÷R`: quotient in $X$, remainder in $Y$) as a direct key. |
| **R3, C5** | `[<-]` *(Same)* | `CLEAR` *(Expanded menu)* | *(Unassigned)* *(HP-32SII: `=` equals)* | Infix `=` is not needed in RPN mode; leaving Right-Shift `[<-]` unassigned prevents accidental clears during fast entry. |
| **R4, C0** | `[XEQ]` *(Same)* | `FN=` *(Same)* | `[↱] [POLY]` *(HP-32SII: no direct key)* | Adds the closed-form quadratic/cubic `[↱] [POLY]` coefficient entry and root solver (`A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, `EXEC`, `CLR`) on `BLUE + XEQ`. |
| **R4, C3** | `[9]` *(Same)* | `[↰] [▸km]` *(HP-32SII: blank)* | `[↱] [▸mi]` *(HP-32SII: blank)* | Adds direct kilometer $\leftrightarrow$ mile unit conversions (`[↰] [▸km]` on `[↰]`, `[↱] [▸mi]` on `[↱]`) on `[9]`. |
| **R7, C1** | `[0]` *(Same)* | `REGS` *(HP-32SII: `INPUT`)* | `VIEW` *(Same)* | Repurposes programming-only `INPUT` to the `REGS` register viewer while keeping single-variable `VIEW` on `[↱]`. |
| **R7, C3** | `[x∥y]` *(HP-32SII: `R/S`)* | `TVM` *(HP-32SII: `PRGM`)* | `PLOT` *(HP-32SII: `PSE`)* | Repurposes `R/S` (`PRGM`/`PSE`) to Primary `[x∥y]`, Left-Shift `TVM` financial solver, Right-Shift `PLOT` canvas, and Alpha `(i)`. |
| **R7, C4** | `[+]` *(Same)* | `[LBL]` *(Restored for `EQN`)* | `[RTN]` *(Same)* | Retains `[LBL]` on Left-Shift `[+]` so stored RPN equations can begin with an explicit single-letter label. |
| **`PARTS` Menu** | Trigger: `Right-Shift [√x]` | HP-32SII: `IP`, `FP`, `ABS` | SC-32 adds `SGN`, `GCD`, `LCM` | Places `SGN`, `GCD`, and `LCM` inside the 6-item `PARTS` softkey menu (`IP`, `FP`, `ABS`, `SGN`, `GCD`, `LCM`; only the elementary SC-6 has physical `GCF`/`LCM` buttons). |
| **`CLEAR` Menu** | Trigger: `Left-Shift [<-]` | HP-32SII: `CLx`, `CLVARS`, `CLΣ`, `ALL` | SC-32: `CLEQN`, `CLVARS`, `CLALL`, `CLΣ`, `CLREGS`, `CLSTK` | Expands `CLEAR` to six softkeys (plus `FIN` inside `TVM` to zero `N`, `I%`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV` while preserving `END`/`BEG`). |
| **`FLAGS` Menu** | Trigger: `Right-Shift [×]` | HP-32SII: `SF n`, `CF n`, `FS? n`, `FC? n` | SC-32 adds `4-LVL`, `8-LVL`, `INF`, `EXAM` | Extends `FLAGS` with selectable stack depth (`4-LVL`, `8-LVL`, `INF`) and proctored `EXAM` lockdown. |
| **`EQN` Mode** | Trigger: `Right-Shift [STO]` | HP-32SII: Infix strings (`SIN(X)+1`) | SC-32: RPN step entry + `EQN_NEW`/`EQN_EDIT` | Stores and edits equations as pure RPN instruction steps with LFU softkeys (`EQN_NEW`, `EQN_EDIT`). |

### C.2.3 Seven Architectural Enhancements Over the Vintage HP-32SII

Beyond the physical keycap legends, the SC-32 expands seven core subsystems while preserving 100% compatibility with classic HP-32SII keystroke sequences:

* **Four-Line Stack Display & Dedicated 6-Key LFU Bar (`R0, C0–C5`):** Replaces the HP-32SII's single-line 12-character LCD with a $132 \times 65\text{ px}$ transflective 4-line stack view ($T, Z, Y, X$) paired with six physical LFU softkeys (`[LFU0]`–`[LFU5]`), so active submenus never hijack `[√x]`..`[Σ+]`.
* **Pure RPN Equations & Iverson Piecewise Booleans (`[↱] [EQN]`):** Evaluates stored equations as pure, side-effect-free RPN token streams rather than infix strings. Relational tests from `[↰] [x?y]` and `[↱] [x?0]` (`R4C4`) act as non-destructive Iverson indicator brackets $[P] \in \{1, 0\}$ on Register $X$ (preserving $Y$ and $Z$) to support branchless piecewise formulas across `[XEQ]`, `[↱] [SOLVE]`, `[↱] [∫]`, and `[↱] [PLOT]`.
* **Direct `|x|` & `÷R` Keys and Expanded `PARTS` Softkey Menu (`R1C0`, `R3C3–C4`):** Reclaiming infix `(` and `)` on Row 3 places Absolute Value `[ABS]` (`|x|`) and Euclidean quotient-remainder division `[↱] [÷R]` on direct right-shifted keys, while the `PARTS` softkey menu (`Right-Shift [√x]`) retains the HP-32SII's `IP`, `FP`, and `ABS` softkeys (`LFU0`–`LFU2`) and adds Signum (`SGN`), Greatest Common Divisor (`GCD`), and Least Common Multiple (`LCM`) on `LFU3`–`LFU5` (unlike the elementary SC-6, where `GCF` and `LCM` are physical keys).
* **Analytic `POLY` Root Workspace & `TVM` Financial Engine (`R4C0`, `R7C3`):** Adds a closed-form quadratic and cubic polynomial solver (`[↱] [POLY]`: `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, `EXEC`, `CLR`) that writes all real and complex conjugate roots to `R34`–`R39`, alongside a 5-variable HP-12C `[↰] [TVM]` solver (`N`, `I%`, `PV`, `PMT`, `FV`, `END/BEG`).
* **128-Column Graphical `PLOT` Viewport (`R7C3`):** Adds a $128 \times 52\text{ px}$ function and statistical scatter-plot canvas with interactive cursor trace (`[↰] [↓]`, `[↰] [↑]`, `[SCRL]`), root-bracketing markers (`MARK`, `STORE`), and shaded definite-integral preview (`∫ f(x)`).
* **Configurable Stack Depth (`4-LVL`, `8-LVL`, `INF`) & Proctored `EXAM` Mode (`R5C4`):** The `FLAGS` menu preserves user Flags `0`–`9` (`SF`, `CF`, `FS?`) and adds the `STACK` submenu (`2-LVL`, `4-LVL`, `8-LVL`, `INF`, `VIEW`) plus proctored `EXAM` lockdown. Default `4-LVL` mode preserves exact Corvallis 4-register physics (including top-of-stack $T$-replication on drop), while `8-LVL` and `INF` (999-level LIFO) eliminate register overflow during deeply nested evaluations.
* **36-Bit Signed Two's-Complement `BASE` Arithmetic & 89-Slot Indirect Memory Map (`i`, `(i)`):** Expands integer `BASE` operations (`DEC`, `HEX`, `OCT`, `BIN`) from 32-bit unsigned truncation to a 36-bit signed two's-complement word (9 hex nibbles, 12 octal digits). Integer pointers $k \in \{1 \dots 89\}$ stored in `i` (`STO` `[.]`) and dereferenced via `(i)` (`RCL` `[x∥y]` or `STO` `[x∥y]`) address:
  * `1`–`26`: Named variables `A` through `Z` (`1 = A`, `2 = B`, $\dots$, `26 = Z`), plus `27` for the index register `i` itself.
  * `28`–`33`: Live statistical accumulators (`n, Σx, Σx², Σy, Σy², Σxy` in the `STATS` register browser; arranged as `Σx, Σy, Σx², Σy², Σxy, n` on the `SUMS` softkey bar).
  * `34`–`39`: Analytic polynomial roots from `[↱] [POLY]` ($\text{Re}(r_1), \text{Im}(r_1), \text{Re}(r_2), \text{Im}(r_2), \text{Re}(r_3), \text{Im}(r_3)$).
  * `40`–`89`: Up to 25 raw statistical data pairs $(x_k, y_k)$ accumulated via `[Σ+]` for scatter plotting (`[↱] [PLOT]`).

## C.3 Open-Source Hardware & Firmware Architecture

Live schematics, Gerber fabrication files, and firmware sources are maintained at [stackcalc.io/hardware](https://stackcalc.io/hardware) and in our public engineering build logs on [Hackaday](https://hackaday.io/project/206743-stackcalc32-a-tactile-rpn-calculator).

### C.3.1 Deterministic State-Machine Execution
The SC-32 firmware is structured around a pure, side-effect-free transition function $\delta(S, k) \to S'$ that separates mathematical state execution from display rendering and matrix scanning. Rather than dispersing stack-lift rules, edit-buffer termination, and error trapping across user-interface handlers, the entire calculator state—comprising the active stack registers, `LASTX`, the 26 named variables (`A`–`Z`), indirect index register `i`, statistical accumulators, `TVM` financial registers, and the Stack Lift flag—resides in a single deterministic value structure.

Maintaining behavioral parity between the physical microcontroller firmware and the desktop/web hardware simulator requires strict adherence to edge-case invariants: how `[ENTER]` disarms stack lift, how an in-progress digit entry interacts with `[x⇄y]`, how `[↰] [LASTX]` captures pre-operation operands differently across unary and dyadic operators, and how pre-mutation domain guards trap $\tan(90^\circ)$ or $\ln(0)$ without corrupting upper registers. Every physical row-and-column switch closure on the handheld PCB steps the formal four-register automaton defined in Appendix A before updating the $132 \times 65$ display buffer.

### C.3.2 Mathematical Rigor in Silicon: Lanczos, Brent, and Romberg
Every transcendental function, statistical estimator, root solver, and definite integral on the SC-32 is implemented using established algorithms from numerical analysis:

* **Continuous Factorials via Cornelius Lanczos's Gamma Approximation:** Rather than limiting `[↰] [x!]` to a lookup table of whole numbers, the engine evaluates $\Gamma(x+1)$ across the real line using Cornelius Lanczos's Chebyshev rational approximation paired with Euler's reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z) = \frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi z)}$, maintaining 15-digit internal precision from fractional half-integers up to $170! \approx 7.2574 \times 10^{306}$.
* **Guaranteed Root-Finding via Richard Brent's Hybrid Algorithm:** Pure Newton–Raphson iteration can diverge when a curve flattens near a local extremum, while pure bisection converges at one binary bit per step. The `[↱] [SOLVE]` engine implements Richard Brent's 1973 hybrid method, which uses inverse quadratic and secant interpolation whenever the iterate converges rapidly and falls back to bisection whenever an iterate would step outside the bracket $[a, b]$ or stall.
* **Adaptive Calculus via Werner Romberg's Richardson Tableau:** When you press `[↱] [∫]`, the calculator constructs a triangular Romberg tableau, halving the trapezoidal step size and applying Lewis Fry Richardson's $\frac{4^m T_{k,m-1} - T_{k-1,m-1}}{4^m - 1}$ error-cancellation cascade to eliminate successive powers of $h^2, h^4, h^6$ until the integral converges to machine tolerance.

Each of these numerical engines—alongside William Kahan's compensated summation and base-preserving percentages, Gaussian complex phasor arithmetic, and 36-bit two's-complement word operations—is verified against reference mathematical test vectors across the full domain.

### C.3.3 Four-Layer Gold-Immersion Hardware, Daylight Optics & Tactile Key-Feel
The physical hardware integrates the PCB switch matrix, reflective optics, and mechanical enclosure as a unified assembly:

* **Four-Layer ENIG Circuit Architecture & Continuous Memory:** The custom four-layer printed circuit board uses an electroless nickel immersion gold (ENIG) surface finish across its switch matrix pads for corrosion-free contact longevity over hundreds of thousands of actuations. Between calculations, the firmware writes atomic, checksum-verified state snapshots—preserving all four stack registers ($T, Z, Y, X$), `LASTX`, the 26 letter registers (`A`–`Z`), all six statistical accumulators, TVM financial registers, and the 24-slot Equation Bank—into alternating non-volatile memory banks.
* **Reflective Daylight Readability & Tactile Snap-Dome Acoustics:** Rather than an emissive smartphone screen that washes out in direct sunlight, the SC-32 pairs a $132 \times 65$ transflective liquid-crystal display with a brushed-aluminum faceplate. Ambient light passes through the liquid-crystal layer and reflects off the internal metallic reflector, increasing contrast as ambient illumination rises, while stainless-steel snap domes beneath the 43 sculpted keycaps provide mechanical tactile feedback on each actuation.
* **Simulating Silicon & Board-Aware Parametric CAD:** During board fabrication, a browser-based hardware simulator wired to a cycle-accurate microcontroller emulator verified matrix debouncing, sleep wake-up timing, and pixel typography before physical bring-up. As documented in the Hackaday engineering logs, the parametric OpenSCAD enclosure scripts read mounting and switch coordinates directly from the KiCad layout—separating mechanical alignment, capture, stop, and release geometries so the tapered chassis, faceplate, TPU keypad membrane, and snap-retained cap assemble without screws or adhesive. Complete KiCad schematics, parametric CAD sources, printable `.stl`/`.3mf` files, and firmware build logs are published at [stackcalc.io/downloads](https://stackcalc.io/downloads) for students, educators, and engineers.

# Appendix D: Mathematical Constants, SI Units & STEM Equations

## D.1 Mathematical Constants, BIPM SI Prefixes & Exact Unit Conversions

One hundred core equations across classical mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, optics, chemistry, astronomy, and finance pair each formula with its physical constants and step-by-step RPN stack execution on the StackCalc SC-32.

### D.1.1 SC-32 Scientific Register Hierarchy & Data Flow

| Register / Bank | Architectural Level | Operational Role & Data Flow |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Register T** | Top / Constant Buffer | Retains constant factor and replicates on dyadic stack drop |
| **Register Z** | Third Stack Level | Holds intermediate sub-expressions and vector/matrix terms |
| **Register Y** | Second Stack Level | Stores waiting dyadic base, dividend, or coordinate component |
| **Register X** | Active / Display | Direct keyboard entry and live computed result readout |
| **LASTX** | Recovery Buffer | Automatically captures previous $X$ before arithmetic/transcendentals |
| **STATS Bank** | 6 Accumulators | Hardware registers $\Sigma x, \Sigma y, \Sigma x^2, \Sigma y^2, \Sigma xy, n$ |
| **Memory A–Z** | 26 Global Registers | Persistent variable storage via `[STO]` and `[RCL]` |

### D.1.2 Scientific Notation, Register Telemetry, and Inside-Out Evaluation
Physical constants spanning dozens of orders of magnitude (such as Planck's constant $6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$) are entered directly via the exponent key (`6.62607015 [E] 34 [+/-]`). As multi-step equations execute, intermediate physical quantities (such as angular frequency $\omega$ in Register $Y$ and capacitance $C$ in Register $X$) remain continuously visible on the $132 \times 65$ transflective LCD, so deeply nested blackbody radiation, thermodynamic, and relativistic formulas collapse inside-out without parentheses or scratchpad registers.

### D.1.3 Fundamental Mathematical & Exact 2019 SI Physical Constants

Under the May 20, 2019 SI Redefinition (26th CGPM), seven defining constants of nature are fixed as exact numerical invariants with zero measurement uncertainty: the vacuum speed of light ($c = 299,792,458\text{ m/s}$), Planck's constant ($h = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$), elementary charge ($e = 1.602176634 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$), Boltzmann's constant ($k_B = 1.380649 \times 10^{-23}\text{ J/K}$), Avogadro's constant ($N_A = 6.02214076 \times 10^{23}\text{ mol}^{-1}$), the molar gas constant ($R = N_A k_B = 8.314462618\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$), and the Stefan–Boltzmann constant ($\sigma = \frac{2\pi^5 k_B^4}{15 c^2 h^3} = 5.670374419 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K}^4)$).

## D.2 Fundamental Equations of Science and Engineering

### D.2.1 Classical Mechanics, Orbital Dynamics & Statics

#### Kinematic Velocity-Displacement Relation
$$v_f = \sqrt{v_i^2 + 2 a \Delta x}$$
Derived by eliminating elapsed time $t$ between the velocity-time and position-time equations, this work-energy identity equates the specific work $a \Delta x$ performed by a constant acceleration $a$ ($\text{m/s}^2$) over a displacement $\Delta x$ ($\text{m}$) to the gain in kinetic energy per unit mass $\frac{1}{2}(v_f^2 - v_i^2)$ from initial speed $v_i$ ($\text{m/s}$). Because $v_f^2$ grows linearly with stopping or takeoff distance $\Delta x$, doubling a vehicle's initial velocity requires four times the braking distance under fixed deceleration.

On the SC-32 stack, squaring $v_i$ in place first and allowing automatic stack lift to hold $v_i^2$ in Register $Y$ while forming $2a\Delta x$ in Register $X$ (`vi [↰] [x²] 2 [ENTER] a [×] dx [×] [+] [√x]`) evaluates the benchmark takeoff roll ($v_i = 12.0\text{ m/s}, a = 4.5\text{ m/s}^2, \Delta x = 25.0\text{ m}$, where $v_i^2 = 144.0\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$ and $2a\Delta x = 225.0\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$) to `19.209373` $\text{m/s}$.

---

#### Projectile Motion Maximum Range
$$R = \frac{v_0^2 \sin(2\theta)}{g}$$
For a projectile launched over level ground in a vacuum with muzzle speed $v_0$ ($\text{m/s}$) and elevation angle $\theta$ (degrees) under standard gravity $g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2$, the horizontal range multiplies the vertical flight time $2v_0\sin\theta / g$ by the constant horizontal ground speed $v_0\cos\theta$. Collapsing $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ through the trigonometric double-angle identity $\sin(2\theta)$ proves both that maximum range occurs at $\theta = 45^\circ$ (where $\sin 90^\circ = 1$) and that complementary launch angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$ strike the exact same downrange point. In `[DEG]` mode, squaring $v_0$ first so it waits in Register $Y$ while doubling and taking the sine of $\theta$ (`v0 [↰] [x²] theta [ENTER] 2 [×] [SIN] [×] 9.80665 [÷]`) resolves $v_0 = 45.0\text{ m/s}$ and $\theta = 35.0^\circ$ ($v_0^2 \sin 70^\circ = 1902.8776\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$) to `194.0395` $\text{m}$.

---

#### Centripetal Acceleration & Radial Force
$$F_c = \frac{m v^2}{r}$$
Christian Huygens proved in *Horologium Oscillatorium* (1673) that deflecting a body of mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) along a circular arc of radius $r$ ($\text{m}$) at constant tangential speed $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) requires a continuous inward radial acceleration $a_c = v^2 / r$ perpendicular to the velocity vector. Because lateral force scales quadratically with speed $v^2$ and inversely with turn radius $r$, doubling cornering velocity quadruples tire lateral shear or turbine blade root tension, whereas doubling the turn radius halves the load. Squaring $v$ immediately in Register $X$ before multiplying by mass and dividing by radius (`v [↰] [x²] m [×] r [÷]`) resolves a cornering vehicle ($m = 1250\text{ kg}, v = 24.0\text{ m/s}, r = 60.0\text{ m}$) via `24 [↰] [x²] 1250 [×] 60 [÷]` to `12000.0` $\text{N}$ ($12.0\text{ kN}$).

---

#### Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
$$F_g = G \frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$$
Isaac Newton's *Principia* (1687) unified terrestrial weight and celestial mechanics by demonstrating that any two spherically symmetric masses $m_1$ and $m_2$ ($\text{kg}$) separated by center-to-center distance $r$ ($\text{m}$) attract each other with a force proportional to the universal gravitational constant $G = 6.67430 \times 10^{-11}\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$. The inverse-square $1/r^2$ geometric dilution reflects conservation of gravitational flux across concentric spherical shells of surface area $4\pi r^2$ in three-dimensional space. Entering the numerator product $G m_1 m_2$ via the scientific exponent key `[E]` and dividing by $r^2$ (`6.67430 [E] 11 [+/-] [ENTER] m1 [×] m2 [×] r [↰] [x²] [÷]`) for an $m_2 = 1500\text{ kg}$ spacecraft orbiting Earth ($m_1 = 5.9722 \times 10^{24}\text{ kg}$) at $r = 6.771 \times 10^6\text{ m}$ yields an orbital attraction of `13041.44` $\text{N}$.

---

#### Circular Orbital Velocity
$$v = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{r}}$$
Equating the inward gravitational pull $\mu / r^2$—where $\mu = GM_\oplus = 3.986004418 \times 10^{14}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}^2$ is Earth's standard geocentric gravitational parameter—to the centripetal acceleration $v^2 / r$ required to maintain a circular orbit of radius $r$ ($\text{m}$) yields the local circular orbital speed. Because $r$ appears in the denominator under the radical, orbital mechanics exhibits the paradoxical property that spacecraft in higher-altitude orbits travel at slower linear velocities than those in low Earth orbit. Dividing $\mu$ by $r$ and extracting the square root in place (`3.986004418 [E] 14 [ENTER] r [÷] [√x]`) for a $400\text{ km}$ Low Earth Orbit ($r = 6.771 \times 10^6\text{ m}$) returns `7672.60` $\text{m/s}$.

---

#### Planetary Escape Velocity
$$v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \mu}{r}} = v_{\text{orbital}} \times \sqrt{2}$$
A spacecraft escapes a central gravitational field of parameter $\mu$ ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$) from radial distance $r$ ($\text{m}$) onto a zero-total-energy parabolic trajectory when its specific kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}v_{\text{esc}}^2$ exactly balances the local gravitational potential well depth $\mu / r$. Regardless of the planet's mass or radius, the local escape speed is always exactly $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41421$ times the circular orbital velocity at that same altitude. Evaluating the quotient under the radical directly on the stack (`2 [ENTER] mu [×] r [÷] [√x]`) from Earth's mean surface radius ($r = 6.371 \times 10^6\text{ m}, \mu = 3.986004418 \times 10^{14}\text{ m}^3/\text{s}^2$) yields `11186.1` $\text{m/s}$ ($11.19\text{ km/s}$).

---

#### Tsiolkovsky Rocket Burnout Equation
$$\Delta v = v_e \ln\left(\frac{m_0}{m_f}\right)$$
Konstantin Tsiolkovsky's 1903 differential momentum integration governs a rocket expelling propellant at effective exhaust velocity $v_e = I_{\text{sp}} g_0$ ($\text{m/s}$) as vehicle mass decreases from initial wet mass $m_0$ to final dry burnout mass $m_f$. Because ideal velocity change $\Delta v$ grows only with the natural logarithm of the mass ratio $m_0 / m_f$, achieving orbital or interplanetary velocities requires either high-specific-impulse propulsion ($v_e$) or staging to jettison empty structural mass along the ascent. Forming the mass ratio in Register $X$, taking `[LN]`, and scaling by $v_e$ (`m0 [ENTER] mf [÷] [LN] ve [×]`) for $v_e = 3100\text{ m/s}, m_0 = 45000\text{ kg}, m_f = 6500\text{ kg}$ yields `5998.07` $\text{m/s}$.

---

#### Rotational Kinetic Energy of Rigid Body
$$E_{\text{rot}} = \frac{1}{2} I \omega^2$$
Summing the translational kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2} dm (\omega r)^2$ of every differential mass element across a rigid rotor replaces linear mass $m$ with the mass moment of inertia $I = \int r^2\,dm$ ($\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$) and linear speed $v$ with angular velocity $\omega$ ($\text{rad/s}$). Because geometric mass distribution scales $I$ with the square of radial distance $r^2$ while spin rate enters as $\omega^2$, energy-storage flywheels and satellite reaction wheels concentrate rim mass at the outer periphery and spin at high angular speeds. Squaring $\omega$ first on Register $X$ and multiplying by $I/2$ (`omega [↰] [x²] I [×] 2 [÷]`) for a rotor with $I = 4.25\text{ kg}\cdot\text{m}^2$ at $\omega = 150.0\text{ rad/s}$ gives `47812.5` $\text{J}$ ($47.81\text{ kJ}$).

---

#### Simple Gravity Pendulum Period
$$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$
Under the small-angle linearization $\sin\theta \approx \theta$, the restoring gravitational torque on a simple pendulum of pivot-to-bob length $L$ ($\text{m}$) in local gravity $g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2$ forms a harmonic oscillator of angular frequency $\omega_0 = \sqrt{g/L}$. As Galileo observed and Christiaan Huygens formalized, the bob mass cancels out of both the gravitational restoring force and the inertial acceleration, so the round-trip period $T$ depends solely on $L$ and $g$. Computing the inner ratio $L/g$, taking its square root, and scaling by $2\pi$ (`L [ENTER] 9.80665 [÷] [√x] 2 [×] [↱] [π] [×]`) for a Huygens seconds pendulum ($L = 0.99362\text{ m}$, beating $1\text{ s}$ per half-swing) confirms $T =$ `2.00000` $\text{s}$.

---

#### Euler Critical Buckling Load for Slender Column
$$P_{\text{cr}} = \frac{\pi^2 E I}{K^2 L^2}$$
Leonhard Euler's 1744 eigenvalue analysis of the elastic elastica shows that a slender compression strut of Young's modulus $E$ ($\text{Pa}$), minimum weak-axis area moment of inertia $I$ ($\text{m}^4$), unsupported length $L$ ($\text{m}$), and effective end-restraint factor $K$ (where $K = 1.0$ for pinned-pinned ends and $K = 0.5$ for fixed-fixed ends) bifurcates into lateral bending long before reaching the material's compressive yield stress. Because the critical load $P_{\text{cr}}$ depends solely on flexural rigidity $EI$ and drops inversely with the square of effective length $(KL)^2$, doubling a column's unbraced span cuts its buckling capacity fourfold.

Forming the numerator $\pi^2 E I$ in Register $Y$ and dividing by $(KL)^2$ (`[↱] [π] [↰] [x²] E [×] I [×] K [ENTER] L [×] [↰] [x²] [÷]`) for a steel column ($E = 200 \times 10^9\text{ Pa}, I = 6.4 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}^4, K = 1.0, L = 4.5\text{ m}$) yields `623856.5` $\text{N}$ ($623.86\text{ kN}$).

---

### D.2.2 Fluid Mechanics, Hydraulics & Aerodynamics


#### Torricelli Efflux Jet Velocity
$$v = \sqrt{2 g h}$$
Evangelista Torricelli demonstrated in 1643—a result later recognized as a direct application of Daniel Bernoulli's streamline energy conservation between a free reservoir surface and an open atmospheric discharge jet—that liquid under hydrostatic head $h$ ($\text{m}$) exits a sharp orifice at the exact speed acquired by a body falling freely from height $h$ under gravity $g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2$. Because efflux velocity grows only with the square root of head $\sqrt{h}$, quadrupling the liquid depth in a gravity-fed tank is required to double the nozzle discharge speed. Multiplying $2g$ by head $h$ and extracting the square root in place (`2 [ENTER] 9.80665 [×] h [×] [√x]`) for a tank head of $h = 5.0\text{ m}$ ($2gh = 98.0665\text{ m}^2/\text{s}^2$) yields `9.90285` $\text{m/s}$.

---

#### Volumetric Flow Continuity Equation
$$Q = A_1 v_1 = \frac{\pi D_1^2}{4} v_1$$
For an incompressible fluid moving through a circular conduit of internal diameter $D_1$ ($\text{m}$) at mean cross-sectional velocity $v_1$ ($\text{m/s}$), conservation of mass requires the volumetric flow rate $Q$ ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}$) to remain invariant across every cross-section ($A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$). Because circular cross-sectional area $A_1 = \frac{\pi}{4}D_1^2$ scales with the square of diameter, tapering a nozzle to half its upstream diameter reduces the flow area fourfold and forces the fluid velocity to quadruple. Squaring $D_1$ first on Register $X$ and scaling by $\frac{\pi}{4} v_1$ (`D [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] 4 [÷] v [×]`) for a $D_1 = 0.15\text{ m}$ supply main flowing at $v_1 = 2.4\text{ m/s}$ yields `0.0424115` $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$ ($42.41\text{ L/s}$).

---

#### Reynolds Number for Pipe Flow
$$Re = \frac{\rho v D}{\mu}$$
Introduced by George Gabriel Stokes and popularized by Osborne Reynolds's 1883 dye-filament pipe experiments, the dimensionless Reynolds number measures the ratio of convective inertial momentum ($\rho v^2 / D$) to Newtonian viscous shear stress ($\mu v / D^2$) for a fluid of density $\rho$ ($\text{kg/m}^3$) and dynamic viscosity $\mu$ ($\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$) flowing at speed $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) through hydraulic diameter $D$ ($\text{m}$). Internal pipe flow remains smooth and laminar below $Re \approx 2300$, passes through an intermittent transitional regime, and becomes fully turbulent with chaotic eddy mixing above $Re \approx 4000$. Chaining the inertial numerator and dividing by viscosity (`rho [ENTER] v [×] D [×] mu [÷]`) for water at $20^\circ\text{C}$ ($\rho = 998\text{ kg/m}^3, v = 1.8\text{ m/s}, D = 0.05\text{ m}, \mu = 0.001002\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$) gives $Re =$ `89640.7` (fully turbulent).

---

#### Darcy-Weisbach Friction Head Loss
$$h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{v^2}{2 g}$$
Formulated by Henry Darcy and Julius Weisbach, this foundational hydraulic loss equation expresses the irreversible pressure head $h_f$ ($\text{m}$ of fluid column) dissipated by wall shear across a pipe of length $L$ ($\text{m}$) and diameter $D$ ($\text{m}$) carrying flow at velocity $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) under gravity $g = 9.80665\text{ m/s}^2$, where $f$ is the dimensionless Darcy friction factor from the Colebrook-White or Moody chart. Because head loss scales with the aspect ratio $L/D$ and the velocity head $v^2 / (2g)$, doubling volumetric throughput in a fixed conduit quadruples frictional pumping head. Evaluating the dimensionless geometric factor $f L / D$ first and multiplying by $v^2 / (2g)$ (`f [ENTER] L [×] D [÷] v [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷] 9.80665 [÷]`) for $f = 0.024, L = 120.0\text{ m}, D = 0.20\text{ m}, v = 2.5\text{ m/s}$ yields $h_f =$ `4.5887` $\text{m}$.

---

#### Manning Formula for Open Channel Uniform Flow
$$v = \frac{1}{n} R_h^{2/3} S^{1/2}$$
Irish engineer Robert Manning's 1889 empirical correlation governs steady, uniform, free-surface gravity flow in aqueducts, storm culverts, and natural riverbeds, balancing the downslope gravitational component $S = \Delta z / L$ against boundary roughness $n$ across a channel of hydraulic radius $R_h = A / P_{\text{wet}}$ ($\text{m}$, the cross-sectional flow area divided by wetted perimeter). Deep, compact channels with a large hydraulic radius $R_h$ minimize wall drag per unit flow area, accelerating mean velocity as $R_h^{2/3}$. Raising $R_h$ to the $\frac{2}{3}$ power via `[yˣ]`, multiplying by $\sqrt{S}$, and dividing by Gauckler–Manning roughness $n$ (`Rh [ENTER] 2 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [yˣ] S [√x] [×] n [÷]`) for a concrete-lined canal ($n = 0.015, R_h = 0.85\text{ m}, S = 0.0025$) produces `2.9911` $\text{m/s}$.

---

#### Poiseuille Laminar Capillary Flow Rate
$$Q = \frac{\pi r^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$
Derived independently by Jean Léonard Marie Poiseuille and Gotthilf Hagen from the exact parabolic velocity profile $u(r)$ of steady laminar flow ($Re < 2300$), this law relates volumetric throughput $Q$ ($\text{m}^3/\text{s}$) to pressure drop $\Delta P$ ($\text{Pa}$) across a cylindrical capillary tube of inner radius $r$ ($\text{m}$) and length $L$ ($\text{m}$) filled with fluid of viscosity $\mu$ ($\text{Pa}\cdot\text{s}$). Because both the cross-sectional area ($\propto r^2$) and the peak centerline velocity ($\propto r^2$) scale quadratically with radius, laminar conductance varies with the fourth power $r^4$—meaning a $16\%$ constriction in a microfluidic channel or coronary artery cuts volumetric flow in half.

Raising $r$ to the fourth power first and chaining the remaining factors (`r [ENTER] 4 [yˣ] [↱] [π] [×] dP [×] 8 [÷] mu [÷] L [÷]`) for $r = 0.002\text{ m}, \Delta P = 5000\text{ Pa}, \mu = 0.0035\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}, L = 0.50\text{ m}$ yields $1.7952 \times 10^{-5}$ $\text{m}^3/\text{s}$.

---

#### Aerodynamic Dynamic Pressure
$$q = \frac{1}{2} \rho v^2$$
In subsonic aerodynamics, dynamic pressure $q$ ($\text{Pa}$) represents the kinetic energy per unit volume of an airstream of density $\rho$ ($\text{kg/m}^3$) moving at true airspeed $v$ ($\text{m/s}$), measured physically as the differential pressure between a forward-facing Pitot stagnation port and a flush static pressure port. Aerodynamic lift $L = q S C_L$ and parasitic drag $D = q S C_D$ scale directly with $q$, explaining why aircraft flying in thin high-altitude air ($\rho \ll \rho_0$) must maintain a much higher true airspeed $v$ to preserve the same indicated dynamic pressure and stall margin. Squaring airspeed $v$ in Register $X$ and multiplying by $\rho / 2$ (`v [↰] [x²] rho [×] 2 [÷]`) at standard sea level ($\rho = 1.225\text{ kg/m}^3, v = 65.0\text{ m/s}$) returns `2587.81` $\text{Pa}$.

---

#### Compressible Flow Mach Number
$$M = \frac{v}{\sqrt{\gamma R_{\text{specific}} T}}$$
Named after Austrian physicist Ernst Mach, the Mach number $M$ normalizes true flight speed $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) by the local speed of sound $a = \sqrt{\gamma R_{\text{specific}} T}$ in an ideal gas of adiabatic index $\gamma = 1.40$, specific gas constant $R_{\text{specific}} = 287.058\text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$ for dry air, and absolute static temperature $T$ ($\text{K}$). Because acoustic wave propagation speed depends exclusively on the square root of absolute temperature $\sqrt{T}$, the speed of sound drops from $340.3\text{ m/s}$ at sea level ($288.15\text{ K}$) to $313.8\text{ m/s}$ in the cold stratosphere ($245.0\text{ K}$), bringing cruising airliners near the transonic compressibility threshold ($M \approx 0.8$).

Computing the acoustic denominator $\sqrt{\gamma R T}$ first in Register $X$, entering $v$, and swapping via `[x⇄y]` (`1.4 [ENTER] 287.058 [×] T [×] [√x] v [x⇄y] [÷]`) for $v = 240.0\text{ m/s}$ at $T = 245.0\text{ K}$ yields Mach `0.7649`.

### D.2.3 Thermodynamics, Gas Laws & Heat Transfer


#### Ideal Gas State Equation
$$P = \frac{n R T}{V}$$
By synthesizing Robert Boyle's isothermal compression law, Jacques Charles's isobaric expansion law, and Amedeo Avogadro's molar volume hypothesis, Émile Clapeyron's ideal gas equation relates the absolute pressure $P$ ($\text{Pa}$) exerted on a vessel of volume $V$ ($\text{m}^3$) to the molar quantity $n$ ($\text{mol}$), the exact 2019 SI molar gas constant $R = N_A k_B = 8.314462618\text{ J/(mol}\cdot\text{K)}$, and the absolute temperature $T$ ($\text{K}$). Microscopically, the numerator $nRT$ measures two-thirds of the total translational kinetic energy of the enclosed gas molecules colliding elastically against the container walls. Chaining the thermal energy product $nRT$ in Register $X$ before dividing by volume $V$ (`n [ENTER] 8.314462618 [×] T [×] V [÷]`) for $n = 4.5\text{ mol}$ at $T = 350.0\text{ K}$ inside $V = 0.035\text{ m}^3$ ($nRT = 13,095.28\text{ J}$) yields `374150.8` $\text{Pa}$ ($374.15\text{ kPa}$).

---

#### Carnot Thermodynamic Cycle Maximum Efficiency
$$\eta_{\text{Carnot}} = 1 - \frac{T_C}{T_H}$$
Sadi Carnot's 1824 treatise *Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu* established that no heat engine operating between a hot thermal reservoir at absolute temperature $T_H$ ($\text{K}$) and a cold rejection sink at $T_C$ ($\text{K}$) can exceed the reversible isothermal-isentropic cycle efficiency $\eta_{\text{Carnot}}$. Because the Second Law of Thermodynamics mandates that entropy extracted from the hot source ($Q_H / T_H$) must be discharged into the cold sink ($Q_C / T_C \ge Q_H / T_H$), achieving $100\%$ thermal efficiency would require either an infinitely hot heat source or an unachievable absolute-zero sink ($T_C = 0\text{ K}$). Computing the absolute temperature ratio $T_C / T_H$ first and subtracting from unity via `[x⇄y]` (`TC [ENTER] TH [÷] 1 [x⇄y] [-]`) for $T_C = 295.0\text{ K}$ and $T_H = 850.0\text{ K}$ yields `0.65294` ($65.29\%$).

---

#### Stefan-Boltzmann Total Radiative Power
$$P = \sigma \epsilon A T^4$$
Derived by Jozef Stefan (1879) and Ludwig Boltzmann (1884) and later anchored to quantum mechanics by integrating Max Planck's spectral blackbody distribution over all frequencies and solid angles, this law expresses the total electromagnetic thermal power $P$ ($\text{W}$) radiated by a body of surface area $A$ ($\text{m}^2$), gray-body emissivity $\epsilon \in (0, 1]$, and absolute temperature $T$ ($\text{K}$), where $\sigma = 5.670374419 \times 10^{-8}\text{ W/(m}^2\cdot\text{K}^4)$. Because radiative emission scales with the fourth power of absolute temperature ($T^4$), doubling the temperature of a vacuum furnace filament or deep-space radiator panel multiplies its radiant heat rejection sixteenfold.

Raising $T$ to the fourth power first and multiplying by $A$, $\epsilon$, and $\sigma$ (`T [ENTER] 4 [yˣ] A [×] eps [×] 5.670374419 [E] 8 [+/-] [×]`) for $T = 1200.0\text{ K}, A = 1.8\text{ m}^2, \epsilon = 0.85$ gives `179898.7` $\text{W}$ ($179.90\text{ kW}$).

---

#### Fourier Conduction Heat Transfer Rate
$$q = \frac{k A (T_1 - T_2)}{L}$$
Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier's 1822 *Théorie analytique de la chaleur* established that steady-state conductive heat flow $q$ ($\text{W}$) across a planar slab of thermal conductivity $k$ ($\text{W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}$), cross-sectional area $A$ ($\text{m}^2$), and thickness $L$ ($\text{m}$) is directly proportional to the face-to-face temperature difference $T_1 - T_2$ ($\text{K}$). Writing the relation in thermal-circuit form $q = (T_1 - T_2) / R_{\text{th}}$ with thermal resistance $R_{\text{th}} = L / (kA)$ provides an exact mathematical parallel to Ohm's law for multi-layer building envelopes, semiconductor package baseplates, and cryogenic Dewar insulation. Forming the temperature drop $T_1 - T_2$ first and scaling by $k A / L$ (`T1 [ENTER] T2 [-] k [×] A [×] L [÷]`) for a masonry wall ($k = 0.75\text{ W/(m}\cdot\text{K)}, A = 15.0\text{ m}^2, L = 0.20\text{ m}$) spanning $T_1 = 295.15\text{ K}$ to $T_2 = 263.15\text{ K}$ yields `1800.0` $\text{W}$.

---

#### Newton's Law of Cooling Transient Temperature
$$T(t) = T_{\infty} + (T_0 - T_{\infty}) e^{-k t}$$
When a thermally conductive body with low internal Biot number ($\text{Bi} = h L_c / k \ll 0.1$) cools or warms from initial temperature $T_0$ in a convective bath of ambient temperature $T_\infty$, its temperature excess $T(t) - T_\infty$ decays exponentially at rate $k = hA / (m c_p)$ ($\text{s}^{-1}$) over elapsed time $t$ ($\text{s}$). Because the instantaneous cooling rate $dT/dt = -k(T - T_\infty)$ is proportional to the remaining thermal excess, each elapsed time constant $\tau = 1/k$ reduces the temperature gap to $e^{-1} \approx 36.79\%$ of its initial value. Evaluating inside-out from the decay factor $e^{-kt}$ outward (`k [+/-] [ENTER] t [×] [eˣ] T0 [ENTER] Tinf [-] [×] Tinf [+]`, or `k [+/-] [ENTER] t [×] [eˣ] N0 [×]` when $T_\infty = 0$) for $T_\infty = 20.0^\circ\text{C}, T_0 = 90.0^\circ\text{C}, k = 0.005\text{ s}^{-1}, t = 180.0\text{ s}$ resolves $T(180) =$ `48.46` $^\circ\text{C}$.

---

#### Logarithmic Mean Temperature Difference (LMTD)
$$\text{LMTD} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$
In a parallel-flow or counterflow heat exchanger where the local fluid-to-fluid temperature approach $\Delta T(x)$ varies from $\Delta T_1$ at the inlet header to $\Delta T_2$ at the outlet header ($\text{K}$ or $^\circ\text{C}$), the local heat flux $dq = U \Delta T(x)\,dA$ causes $\Delta T(x)$ to decay exponentially along the exchanger length. Integrating that exponential profile yields the logarithmic mean temperature difference $\text{LMTD}$ for $q = U A \cdot \text{LMTD}$, which is always strictly less than the simple arithmetic average $(\Delta T_1 + \Delta T_2)/2$ whenever $\Delta T_1 \ne \Delta T_2$. Computing the terminal difference $\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2$ in Register $Y$ and dividing by the natural logarithm of the terminal ratio $\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)$ (`dT1 [ENTER] dT2 [-] dT1 [ENTER] dT2 [÷] [LN] [÷]`) for $\Delta T_1 = 45.0\text{ K}$ and $\Delta T_2 = 18.0\text{ K}$ gives `29.4665` $\text{K}$.

---

#### Ideal Brayton Gas Turbine Thermal Efficiency
$$\eta = 1 - \frac{1}{r_p^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma}}$$
Named after George Brayton, the ideal open or closed gas-turbine power cycle compresses intake gas isentropically across pressure ratio $r_p = P_2 / P_1$, adds heat at constant pressure in the combustor, and expands the hot gas isentropically through a power turbine, where $\gamma = c_p / c_v$ is the specific-heat ratio ($\gamma = 1.40$ for diatomic air). Because the isentropic temperature ratio across the compressor equals $T_2 / T_1 = r_p^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$, raising the overall compressor pressure ratio $r_p$ directly increases thermal efficiency and explains why modern turbofan cores operate at pressure ratios exceeding $40:1$. Forming the exponent $(\gamma - 1)/\gamma$ on the stack, raising $r_p$ via `[yˣ]`, taking the reciprocal, and subtracting from unity (`rp [ENTER] 1.4 [ENTER] 1 [-] 1.4 [÷] [yˣ] [1/x] 1 [x⇄y] [-]`) at $r_p = 16.0$ and $\gamma = 1.40$ yields `0.5471` ($54.71\%$).

---

#### Latent Heat Phase Transition Energy
$$Q = m L_v$$
Discovered by Joseph Black in 1761, latent heat $Q$ ($\text{J}$) represents the isothermal enthalpy required to break or reform intermolecular bonds across a first-order phase transition of mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) with specific latent heat of vaporization (or fusion) $L_v$ ($\text{J/kg}$) while the thermodynamic temperature remains pinned at the boiling or melting point. Water's exceptionally high hydrogen-bond enthalpy of vaporization ($L_v = 2.26 \times 10^6\text{ J/kg}$ at $100^\circ\text{C}$—more than five times the sensible heat needed to warm liquid water from $0^\circ\text{C}$ to $100^\circ\text{C}$) underpins industrial steam Rankine boilers, heat pipes, and evaporative cooling towers. Multiplying mass $m$ by $L_v$ (`m [ENTER] Lv [×]`) for $m = 2.5\text{ kg}$ of boiling water at $100^\circ\text{C}$ yields `5650000.0` $\text{J}$ ($5.65\text{ MJ}$).

### D.2.4 Electricity, Magnetism & AC Circuit Analysis


#### Ohm's Law and DC Power Dissipation
$$P = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R} = V I$$
Combining Georg Simon Ohm's linear conduction law ($V = IR$) with James Prescott Joule's calorimetric heating law ($P = VI$) expresses the thermal power $P$ ($\text{W}$) dissipated in a resistive load $R$ ($\Omega$) under terminal voltage $V$ ($\text{V}$) and current $I$ ($\text{A}$). Because $P = V^2 / R$ scales quadratically with applied voltage across a fixed resistance (and $P = I^2 R$ scales quadratically with line current along a transmission cable), doubling supply voltage quadruples resistive heating, whereas stepping transmission voltage up tenfold reduces $I^2 R$ grid losses a hundredfold for the same delivered power. Squaring $V$ in Register $X$ and dividing by $R$ (`V [↰] [x²] R [÷]`) for a $V = 120.0\text{ V}$ heating element of resistance $R = 15.0\,\Omega$ yields `960.0` $\text{W}$.

---

#### Equivalent Resistance of Parallel Networks via x∥y
$$R_{\text{eq}} = R_1 \parallel R_2 \parallel R_3 = \frac{1}{\frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}}$$
When resistive branches $R_1, R_2, R_3$ ($\Omega$) share a common terminal node pair, Kirchhoff's current law dictates that their individual conductances $G_i = 1 / R_i$ ($\text{S}$) sum linearly, so the combined equivalent resistance $R_{\text{eq}}$ is always strictly smaller than the smallest individual branch resistor. Rather than keying three reciprocals, two additions, and a final reciprocal, the SC-32's dedicated hardware parallel operator `[x∥y]` evaluates $X \cdot Y / (X + Y)$ in a single keystroke and associatively chains across any number of branches. Keying `R1 [ENTER] R2 [x∥y] R3 [x∥y]` for $R_1 = 100.0\,\Omega, R_2 = 150.0\,\Omega, R_3 = 300.0\,\Omega$ collapses $100 \parallel 150 = 60.0\,\Omega$ on the first press and $60 \parallel 300 =$ `50.0` $\Omega$ on the second.

---

#### Electrostatic Energy Stored in Capacitor
$$U_C = \frac{1}{2} C V^2$$
Charging a capacitor of capacitance $C$ ($\text{F}$) to terminal voltage $V$ ($\text{V}$) requires moving incremental charge $dq = C\,dv$ against the rising potential $v$, so integrating $\int_0^V C v\,dv$ yields the stored electrostatic field energy $U_C$ ($\text{J}$) with its characteristic factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ (the remaining half of the energy $C V^2$ supplied by a fixed-voltage DC source is dissipated as heat in the charging resistance). Because stored energy scales quadratically with voltage $V^2$, high-voltage pulsed-laser flashlamp banks, medical defibrillators, and EV traction-inverter DC-link capacitors pack substantial energy into compact dielectric volumes. Squaring $V$ first on Register $X$ and multiplying by $C/2$ (`V [↰] [x²] C [×] 2 [÷]`) for a $C = 47.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$ bus capacitor charged to $V = 450.0\text{ V}$ gives `4.75875` $\text{J}$.

---

#### Magnetic Energy Stored in Inductor
$$U_L = \frac{1}{2} L I^2$$
As the electromagnetic dual of a capacitor's electric field energy, establishing a current $I$ ($\text{A}$) through an inductor of self-inductance $L$ ($\text{H}$) requires doing work against Faraday's counter-EMF $v_L = L\,di/dt$, integrating $\int_0^I L i\,di$ into magnetic flux energy $U_L$ ($\text{J}$) stored within the core air gap and winding field. Because magnetic energy scales with $I^2$ and cannot change discontinuously without generating a destructive voltage spike ($v_L = L\,di/dt$), buck/boost switching regulators and solenoid drivers require freewheeling diodes or synchronous switches to commutate inductor current safely. Squaring $I$ in place and scaling by $L/2$ (`I [↰] [x²] L [×] 2 [÷]`) for an $L = 0.25\text{ H}$ filter choke carrying $I = 6.4\text{ A}$ yields `5.12` $\text{J}$.

---

#### RC Transient Charging Voltage
$$V_C(t) = V_0 \left(1 - e^{-t / (R C)}\right)$$
Applying a step supply voltage $V_0$ ($\text{V}$) through series resistance $R$ ($\Omega$) into an initially uncharged capacitor $C$ ($\text{F}$) produces a first-order differential relaxation governed by the time constant $\tau = R C$ ($\text{s}$). As the capacitor voltage $V_C(t)$ rises, the voltage drop $V_0 - V_C(t)$ driving charging current through $R$ decays exponentially, bringing $V_C(t)$ to $63.21\%$ of $V_0$ at $t = 1\tau$, $95.02\%$ at $t = 3\tau$, and $99.33\%$ at $t = 5\tau$. Evaluating from the dimensionless exponent $-t / (RC)$ outward (`t [+/-] [ENTER] R [÷] C [÷] [eˣ] [+/-] 1 [+] V0 [×]`) for $V_0 = 12.0\text{ V}, R = 10000.0\,\Omega, C = 220.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}$ ($\tau = 2.2\text{ s}$) at $t = 3.5\text{ s}$ gives `9.5551` $\text{V}$.

---

#### RL Inductive Current Decay
$$I(t) = I_0 e^{-t (R / L)}$$
When an inductor $L$ ($\text{H}$) carrying steady initial current $I_0$ ($\text{A}$) is switched across a dissipative loop resistance $R$ ($\Omega$) at $t = 0$, its collapsing magnetic flux sustains current that decays exponentially with inductive time constant $\tau = L / R$ ($\text{s}$). Unlike an RC circuit where larger resistance slows the transient ($\tau = RC$), increasing loop resistance $R$ in an RL flyback path dissipates stored magnetic energy $\frac{1}{2}LI_0^2$ faster and shortens the decay time constant $\tau = L/R$. Forming the negative exponent $-t R / L$ first and scaling by $I_0$ (`t [+/-] [ENTER] R [×] L [÷] [eˣ] I0 [×]`, or `t [+/-] [ENTER] R [×] L [÷] [eˣ] [+/-] 1 [+] V [×] R [÷]` for step energization) for $I_0 = 5.0\text{ A}, R = 24.0\,\Omega, L = 0.80\text{ H}$ at $t = 0.05\text{ s}$ yields `1.1157` $\text{A}$.

---

#### LC Resonant Frequency
$$f_0 = \frac{1}{2 \pi \sqrt{L C}}$$
William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) derived in 1853 that an undamped tank circuit of inductance $L$ ($\text{H}$) and capacitance $C$ ($\text{F}$) exchanges energy harmonically between its magnetic and electric fields at the natural frequency $f_0$ ($\text{Hz}$) where inductive reactance $X_L = 2\pi f_0 L$ and capacitive reactance $X_C = 1 / (2\pi f_0 C)$ are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase. Because $f_0$ varies inversely with $\sqrt{LC}$, sweeping a variable tuning capacitor across a four-to-one capacitance ratio tunes an AM or HF radio receiver across a two-to-one frequency octave. Multiplying $L$ by $C$, taking `[√x]`, scaling by $2\pi$, and inverting via `[1/x]` (`L [ENTER] C [×] [√x] 2 [×] [↱] [π] [×] [1/x]`) for $L = 10.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}$ and $C = 100.0 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F}$ ($\sqrt{LC} = 1.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ s}$) yields `159154.9` $\text{Hz}$ ($159.15\text{ kHz}$).

---

#### RLC Series AC Total Impedance
$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + \left(2 \pi f L - \frac{1}{2 \pi f C}\right)^2}$$
In steady-state sinusoidal AC analysis at frequency $f$ ($\text{Hz}$), a series branch of resistance $R$ ($\Omega$), inductance $L$ ($\text{H}$), and capacitance $C$ ($\text{F}$) presents complex impedance $\mathbf{Z} = R + j(X_L - X_C)$, where inductive reactance $X_L = 2\pi f L$ leads current by $+90^\circ$ and capacitive reactance $X_C = 1/(2\pi f C)$ lags by $-90^\circ$. Because the two reactive components lie $180^\circ$ apart along the imaginary axis, they partially or completely cancel each other before combining in quadrature with real resistance $R$. Storing angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$ in register `A` to evaluate $X_L - X_C$ without re-keying $2\pi f$ (`2 [↱] [π] [×] f [×] [STO] A L [×] [RCL] A C [×] [1/x] [-] [↰] [x²] R [↰] [x²] [+] [√x]`) for $R = 50.0\,\Omega, L = 0.05\text{ H}, C = 10.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ F}, f = 120.0\text{ Hz}$ gives `107.293` $\Omega$.

---

#### Quality Factor of Resonant Circuit
$$Q = \frac{1}{R} \sqrt{\frac{L}{C}}$$
Introduced by K. S. Johnson at Western Electric in 1914, the dimensionless quality factor $Q$ of a series RLC resonator measures $2\pi$ times the ratio of peak energy stored in the reactive tank to the energy dissipated per cycle in series resistance $R$ ($\Omega$), expressed directly as the characteristic impedance $\sqrt{L/C}$ divided by $R$. High-$Q$ resonators exhibit both sharp spectral selectivity—with half-power ($-3\text{ dB}$) fractional bandwidth $\Delta f / f_0 = 1/Q$—and a resonant voltage magnification across $L$ and $C$ equal to $Q$ times the source excitation voltage. Computing the characteristic impedance $\sqrt{L/C}$ first and dividing by $R$ (`L [ENTER] C [÷] [√x] R [÷]`) for $R = 8.0\,\Omega, L = 2.5 \times 10^{-3}\text{ H}, C = 47.0 \times 10^{-9}\text{ F}$ yields $Q =$ `28.829`.

---

#### Decibel Power Gain Ratio
$$\text{dB} = 10 \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)$$
Originated at Bell Telephone Laboratories in the 1920s to quantify signal loss per mile of standard telephone cable, the decibel ($\text{dB}$, one-tenth of a bel) expresses the ratio of output power $P_2$ ($\text{W}$) to reference input power $P_1$ ($\text{W}$) on a base-$10$ logarithmic scale. Mapping power ratios through $10\log_{10}(\cdot)$ converts long chains of cascaded RF amplifier gains, mixer conversion losses, and waveguide attenuations from multi-step multiplications into simple algebraic additions ($+3.0103\text{ dB}$ per power doubling and $+10\text{ dB}$ per decade). Dividing $P_2$ by $P_1$, pressing `[↰] [LOG]`, and scaling by $10$ (`P2 [ENTER] P1 [÷] [↰] [LOG] 10 [×]`) for $P_1 = 0.025\text{ W}$ amplified to $P_2 = 120.0\text{ W}$ gives `36.8124` $\text{dB}$.

### D.2.5 Wave Mechanics, Acoustics & Physical Optics


#### Snell's Law of Refraction
$$\theta_2 = \arcsin\left(\frac{n_1 \sin\theta_1}{n_2}\right)$$
First discovered by Ibn Sahl in 984 CE and rediscovered by Willebrord Snellius in 1621, Snell's law follows from Pierre de Fermat's principle of least optical time across a boundary separating dielectric media of refractive indices $n_1 = c / v_1$ and $n_2 = c / v_2$. Continuity of tangential phase velocity along the interface forces an incident ray at angle $\theta_1$ (measured from the surface normal) to bend toward the normal when entering a denser medium ($n_2 > n_1$) and causes total internal reflection when propagating from a denser to a rarer medium at angles where $(n_1 / n_2)\sin\theta_1 > 1$. In `[DEG]` mode, taking $\sin\theta_1$, scaling by the index ratio $n_1 / n_2$, and applying `[↰] [ASIN]` (`theta1 [SIN] n1 [×] n2 [÷] [↰] [ASIN]`) for a beam entering crown glass ($n_2 = 1.52$) from air ($n_1 = 1.0003$) at $\theta_1 = 45.0^\circ$ gives `27.7297` $^\circ$.

---

#### Gaussian Thin Lens Equation via x∥y
$$f = \frac{d_o \cdot d_i}{d_o + d_i} = d_o \parallel d_i$$
In Carl Friedrich Gauss's paraxial optics approximation, a thin converging lens of focal length $f$ adds optical power $1/f$ to the diverging spherical wavefront curvature $1/d_o$ from an object at distance $d_o$ to focus a real conjugate image at distance $d_i$ according to $1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$. Because the reciprocal sum of conjugate distances is algebraically identical to two parallel resistors, the SC-32's hardware `[x∥y]` operator solves thin-lens and spherical-mirror imaging in a single keystroke without reciprocals. Entering `do [ENTER] di [x∥y]` for an object at $d_o = 30.0\text{ cm}$ projecting a real image at $d_i = 60.0\text{ cm}$ directly returns the focal length $f =$ `20.0` $\text{cm}$.

---

#### Compound Optical Microscope Magnification
$$M = -\left(\frac{L_{\text{tube}}}{f_{\text{obj}}}\right) \left(\frac{d_{\text{near}}}{f_{\text{eye}}}\right)$$
A standard compound microscope achieves high overall angular magnification $M$ by cascading two positive lens stages separated by the mechanical tube length $L_{\text{tube}} = 160\text{ mm}$: a short-focal-length objective lens ($f_{\text{obj}}$, $\text{mm}$) projects a real, inverted intermediate image magnified laterally by $-L_{\text{tube}} / f_{\text{obj}}$, and an eyepiece ($f_{\text{eye}}$, $\text{mm}$) acts as a simple magnifier referenced to the human eye's relaxed near point $d_{\text{near}} = 250\text{ mm}$. Multiplying the objective's lateral magnification by the ocular's angular magnification (`160 [ENTER] fobj [÷] 250 [ENTER] feye [÷] [×] [+/-]`) for an $f_{\text{obj}} = 4.0\text{ mm}$ ($40\times$) objective paired with an $f_{\text{eye}} = 25.0\text{ mm}$ ($10\times$) ocular yields `-400.0` ($\times 400$ inverted angular magnification).

---

#### Acoustic Doppler Frequency Shift (Moving Source)
$$f' = f_0 \left(\frac{v}{v - v_s}\right)$$
Christian Doppler's 1842 principle explains why an acoustic source emitting at rest frequency $f_0$ ($\text{Hz}$) while advancing toward a stationary observer at speed $v_s$ ($\text{m/s}$) through air of sound speed $v = 343.0\text{ m/s}$ crowds successive wave crests closer together in space. Because the emitter chases its own outgoing wavefronts, the compressed wavelength ahead of the source shrinks to $\lambda' = (v - v_s)/f_0$, raising the observed pitch $f' = v / \lambda'$ hyperbolically until wavefronts pile up into a Mach-1 shock cone as $v_s \to v$. Forming the relative velocity $v - v_s$ first, dividing into $v$ via `[x⇄y]`, and scaling by $f_0$ (`343 [ENTER] vs [-] 343 [x⇄y] [÷] f0 [×]`) for an $f_0 = 500.0\text{ Hz}$ train horn approaching at $v_s = 35.0\text{ m/s}$ returns `556.818` $\text{Hz}$.

---

#### Sound Pressure Decibel Level
$$L_p = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_{\text{rms}}}{P_0}\right)$$
Acoustic Sound Pressure Level ($L_p$, in $\text{dB SPL}$) compares the root-mean-square pressure fluctuation $P_{\text{rms}}$ ($\text{Pa}$) of a sound wave against the internationally standardized threshold of human hearing at $1\text{ kHz}$, $P_0 = 20.0 \times 10^{-6}\text{ Pa}$ ($20\text{ }\mu\text{Pa}$). Because acoustic power intensity $I = P_{\text{rms}}^2 / (\rho c)$ is proportional to the square of pressure amplitude, the $10\log_{10}(I / I_0)$ power-ratio definition pulls the exponent of $2$ out front to become $20\log_{10}(P_{\text{rms}} / P_0)$, where every tenfold increase in pressure corresponds to $+20\text{ dB}$. Dividing $P_{\text{rms}}$ by $20\text{ }\mu\text{Pa}$, pressing `[↰] [LOG]`, and multiplying by $20$ (`Prms [ENTER] 20 [E] 6 [+/-] [÷] [↰] [LOG] 20 [×]`) at $P_{\text{rms}} = 0.632\text{ Pa}$ gives `90.0` $\text{dB}$ SPL.

---

#### Sabine Reverberation Time for Architectural Enclosure
$$RT_{60} = \frac{0.161 V}{A_{\text{total}}}$$
Pioneering architectural acoustician Wallace Clement Sabine established in 1898 that the reverberation time $RT_{60}$ ($\text{s}$)—the duration required for diffuse reverberant sound energy in a room of volume $V$ ($\text{m}^3$) to decay by $60\text{ dB}$ (one-millionth of its initial intensity) after a source stops—is directly proportional to room volume and inversely proportional to the effective absorption area $A_{\text{total}} = \sum S_i \alpha_i$ (in metric sabins, $\text{m}^2$). Physically, a larger room volume increases the mean free path $4V/S$ between wall reflections, whereas acoustic panels of high absorption coefficient $\alpha_i$ drain energy faster at each bounce (with empirical constant $0.161\text{ s/m}$ at $20^\circ\text{C}$). Multiplying $0.161$ by $V$ and dividing by $A_{\text{total}}$ (`0.161 [ENTER] V [×] Atot [÷]`) for a recital hall of $V = 850.0\text{ m}^3$ and $A_{\text{total}} = 110.0\text{ sabins}$ yields `1.244` $\text{s}$.

---

#### Optical Diffraction Grating Wavelength
$$\lambda = \frac{d \sin\theta}{m}$$
When collimated light illuminates a diffraction grating ruled with periodic slit spacing $d$ ($\text{m}$), each groove acts as a coherent Huygens secondary wavelet emitter across all outgoing angles $\theta$ (degrees). Adjacent wavelets interfere constructively only at discrete angles where their geometric path-length difference $d\sin\theta$ equals an integer multiple $m\lambda$ ($m = \pm 1, \pm 2, \dots$) of the optical wavelength $\lambda$ ($\text{m}$), dispersing polychromatic light into separated spectral orders. In `[DEG]` mode, evaluating $\sin\theta$ first, multiplying by grating pitch $d$, and dividing by order $m$ (`theta [SIN] d [×] m [÷]`) for a $600\text{ lines/mm}$ grating ($d = 1.6667 \times 10^{-6}\text{ m}$) at first-order angle $\theta = 22.45^\circ$ ($m = 1$) determines $\lambda =$ $6.365 \times 10^{-7}$ $\text{m}$ ($636.5\text{ nm}$).

#### Numerical Aperture of Optical Fiber
$$NA = \sqrt{n_{\text{core}}^2 - n_{\text{clad}}^2}$$
For a step-index optical fiber with core refractive index $n_{\text{core}}$ surrounded by lower-index cladding $n_{\text{clad}}$, Snell's law at the entrance face combined with the critical angle $\sin\theta_c = n_{\text{clad}} / n_{\text{core}}$ at the core-cladding wall defines the dimensionless Numerical Aperture $NA = n_0 \sin\theta_{\max}$. Any ray entering the fiber end-face within the acceptance cone half-angle $\theta_{\max} = \arcsin(NA)$ strikes the internal core wall shallower than the critical angle and propagates down the waveguide via lossless total internal reflection. ### D.2.6 Nuclear, Atomic & Relativistic Physics


#### Einstein Mass-Energy Equivalence
$$E = m c^2$$
Albert Einstein's September 1905 paper demonstrated that rest mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) is a concentrated reservoir of internal energy $E$ ($\text{J}$) scaled by the square of the exact vacuum speed of light $c = 299,792,458\text{ m/s}$, representing the zero-momentum case of the relativistic energy-momentum invariant $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$. Because the conversion factor $c^2 = 8.98755179 \times 10^{16}\text{ J/kg}$ is immense, a nuclear fission or fusion reaction that converts even a tiny mass defect $\Delta m$ of $1.0\text{ gram}$ ($1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$) into kinetic and radiative energy releases macroscopic power on the scale of a city's daily electrical consumption. Squaring $c$ in Register $X$ and multiplying by $m$ (`299792458 [↰] [x²] m [×]`) for $m = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ kg}$ yields $8.98755 \times 10^{13}$ $\text{J}$ ($89.88\text{ TJ}$).

---

#### Planck-Einstein Photon Energy
$$E_{\text{photon}} = \frac{h c}{\lambda}$$
Max Planck's 1900 resolution of the ultraviolet blackbody catastrophe and Albert Einstein's 1905 explanation of the photoelectric effect established that electromagnetic radiation of wavelength $\lambda$ ($\text{m}$) and frequency $\nu = c / \lambda$ is emitted and absorbed in discrete quanta of energy $E_{\text{photon}} = h\nu$, where $h = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$ and $c = 299,792,458\text{ m/s}$. Because photon energy varies inversely with wavelength $\lambda$, a single short-wavelength ultraviolet or X-ray photon can eject a bound inner-shell electron that no intensity of long-wavelength infrared illumination could ever dislodge.

Forming the universal constant product $hc = 1.98644586 \times 10^{-25}\text{ J}\cdot\text{m}$ on the stack and dividing by $\lambda$ (`6.62607015 [E] 34 [+/-] [ENTER] 299792458 [×] lambda [÷]`) for a green photon ($\lambda = 500.0 \times 10^{-9}\text{ m}$) yields $3.9729 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{J}$ ($2.48\text{ eV}$).

---

#### de Broglie Particle Wavelength
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{m v}$$
In his 1924 doctoral thesis, Louis de Broglie extended wave-particle duality from massless photons ($p = h/\lambda$) to massive matter particles, proposing that any particle of mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) moving at non-relativistic speed $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) with momentum $p = mv$ possesses an intrinsic matter-wave wavelength $\lambda = h / p$, where $h = 6.62607015 \times 10^{-34}\text{ J}\cdot\text{s}$. While macroscopic objects have immeasurably small wavelengths, electrons accelerated across kilovolt potentials exhibit sub-nanometer de Broglie wavelengths shorter than interatomic crystal spacings and support atomic-scale diffraction and transmission electron microscopy. Dividing Planck's constant $h$ sequentially by mass $m$ and velocity $v$ (`6.62607015 [E] 34 [+/-] [ENTER] m [÷] v [÷]`) for an electron ($m = 9.1093837 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$) traveling at $v = 2.0 \times 10^6\text{ m/s}$ gives $3.6370 \times 10^{-10}$ $\text{m}$ ($0.3637\text{ nm}$).

#### Relativistic Lorentz Factor ($\gamma$)
$$\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \beta^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}}$$
Hendrik Lorentz and Albert Einstein showed that invariance of the spacetime interval $ds^2 = (c\,dt)^2 - dx^2$ across inertial reference frames moving at relative velocity $v$ requires scaling time and space coordinates by the Lorentz factor $\gamma$, parameterized by the dimensionless speed ratio $\beta = v / c \in [0, 1)$. Near everyday speeds ($\beta \ll 1$), $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}\beta^2$ is indistinguishable from unity, but as $\beta \to 1$, $\gamma$ diverges toward infinity—dilating the proper lifetime $\Delta t = \gamma \Delta\tau$ of high-energy atmospheric muons and contracting longitudinal lengths $L = L_0 / \gamma$. Squaring $\beta$ in Register $X$, subtracting from $1$ via `[x⇄y]`, taking `[√x]`, and inverting via `[1/x]` (`beta [↰] [x²] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [√x] [1/x]`) at $\beta = 0.95$ ($1 - \beta^2 = 0.0975$) computes $\gamma =$ `3.20256`.

#### Relativistic Momentum
$$p = \gamma m v = \frac{m v}{\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}}$$
In special relativity, conservation of four-momentum across collisions requires the spatial momentum of a particle of rest mass $m$ ($\text{kg}$) moving at speed $v$ ($\text{m/s}$) to scale with the Lorentz factor as $p = \gamma m v$ rather than the Newtonian $mv$. As $v$ approaches the speed of light $c = 299,792,458\text{ m/s}$, continuous force application ($F = dp/dt$) pumps energy into the diverging $\gamma$ factor rather than pushing $v$ past $c$, which directly determines the magnetic bending rigidity $B\rho = p / q$ required to steer relativistic protons inside a synchrotron ring. Computing the radical $\sqrt{1 - (v/c)^2}$ first, forming $mv$, and dividing via `[x⇄y]` (`v [ENTER] 299792458 [÷] [↰] [x²] 1 [x⇄y] [-] [√x] m [ENTER] v [×] [x⇄y] [÷]`) for a proton ($m = 1.67262 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$) at $v = 0.85 c = 2.548236 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$ yields $8.0906 \times 10^{-19}$ $\text{kg}\cdot\text{m/s}$.

#### Radioactive Decay Exponential Law
$$N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} = N_0 \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t / t_{1/2}}$$
Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy established in 1902 that radioactive transmutation is a memoryless quantum tunneling process in which each unstable nucleus has a constant probability $\lambda = \ln(2) / t_{1/2}$ per unit time of decaying, independent of its age. Integrating $dN/dt = -\lambda N$ from an initial population or activity $N_0$ over elapsed time $t$ shows that every elapsed half-life $t_{1/2}$ reduces the surviving radioisotope inventory by an exact factor of two. Raising $0.5$ to the elapsed half-life count $t / t_{1/2}$ and scaling by $N_0$ (`0.5 [ENTER] t [ENTER] thalf [÷] [yˣ] N0 [×]`, or `k [+/-] [ENTER] t [×] [eˣ] N0 [×]` when given decay rate $k = \lambda$) for a Cobalt-60 source ($N_0 = 10000.0\text{ Bq}, t_{1/2} = 5.27\text{ years}$) after $t = 15.0\text{ years}$ returns `1390.5` $\text{Bq}$.

#### Rydberg Equation for Hydrogen Spectral Series
$$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R_{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$
Formulated empirically by Johannes Rydberg in 1888 and derived from first principles by Niels Bohr's 1913 quantized angular-momentum model of the hydrogen atom, this relation gives the vacuum wavelength $\lambda$ ($\text{m}$) of photons emitted or absorbed when an electron transitions between principal quantum shells $n_1$ and $n_2$ ($n_1 < n_2$), where $R_\infty = \frac{m_e e^4}{8 \varepsilon_0^2 h^3 c} = 1.0973731568 \times 10^7\text{ m}^{-1}$. Because bound orbital energies scale inversely with the square of the shell index ($E_n = -13.6\text{ eV}/n^2$), transitions terminating on $n_1 = 1, 2, 3$ generate the ultraviolet Lyman, visible Balmer, and infrared Paschen series respectively.

### D.2.7 Coordinate Geometry & Planar Mensuration


#### Volume and Surface Area of Sphere
$$V = \frac{4}{3} \pi r^3, \quad A = 4 \pi r^2$$
In *On the Sphere and Cylinder* (c. 225 BCE)—the geometric ratio Archimedes regarded as his crowning achievement—he proved that a sphere of radius $r$ occupies exactly two-thirds of the volume ($\pi r^2 \cdot 2r = 2\pi r^3$) and two-thirds of the total closed surface area ($2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r \cdot 2r = 6\pi r^2$) of its circumscribing right circular cylinder. Differentiating $V(r) = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ with respect to $r$ recovers $dV/dr = 4\pi r^2 = A$, because an infinitesimal radial expansion $dr$ adds a spherical shell of volume $A\,dr$. Cubing $r$ on the stack via `r [ENTER] 3 [yˣ] [↱] [π] [×] 4 [×] 3 [÷]` for volume and squaring via `r [↰] [x²] [↱] [π] [×] 4 [×]` for surface area at $r = 7.50\text{ cm}$ ($r^3 = 421.875\text{ cm}^3$) yields Volume = `1767.146` $\text{cm}^3$ and Area = `706.858` $\text{cm}^2$.

#### Right Circular Cone Volume & Lateral Surface Area
$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi r^2 h, \quad A_{\text{lat}} = \pi r \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$$
First established by Eudoxus of Cnidus via the method of exhaustion, a right circular cone of base radius $r$ and perpendicular altitude $h$ encloses exactly one-third the volume of its bounding cylinder $\pi r^2 h$ because horizontal cross-sectional disks shrink quadratically with distance from the apex ($\int_0^h (z/h)^2 dz = h/3$). Unrolling the conical sheet along a generator of Pythagorean slant height $\ell = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$ produces a planar circular sector of radius $\ell$ and arc length $2\pi r$, whose area is $\frac{1}{2}(2\pi r)\ell = \pi r\sqrt{r^2 + h^2}$. Evaluating volume via `r [↰] [x²] h [×] [↱] [π] [×] 3 [÷]` and lateral area via `r [↰] [x²] h [↰] [x²] [+] [√x] r [×] [↱] [π] [×]` for $r = 6.0\text{ cm}$ and $h = 14.0\text{ cm}$ returns Volume = `527.788` $\text{cm}^3$ and Lateral Area = `287.108` $\text{cm}^2$.

#### Frustum of Right Circular Cone Volume
$$V = \frac{1}{3} \pi h (R^2 + R r + r^2)$$
Slicing a right circular cone parallel to its base at height $h$ leaves a conical frustum bounded by lower radius $R$ and upper radius $r$—the circular counterpart of the ancient Egyptian Moscow Mathematical Papyrus (Problem 14, c. 1850 BCE) pyramidal frustum. Rather than multiplying $h$ by the arithmetic mean of the two end disks, exact integration over the linearly tapering radius $r(z)$ averages three equally weighted disks: the bottom base $\pi R^2$, the top base $\pi r^2$, and their geometric mean $\pi Rr$. Accumulating the quadratic sum $R^2 + Rr + r^2$ in Register $X$ before scaling by $\frac{1}{3}\pi h$ (`R [↰] [x²] R [ENTER] r [×] [+] r [↰] [x²] [+] h [×] 3 [÷] [↱] [π] [×]`) for $R = 8.0\text{ cm}, r = 3.0\text{ cm}, h = 12.0\text{ cm}$ ($R^2 + Rr + r^2 = 97.0\text{ cm}^2$) yields `1218.938` $\text{cm}^3$.

#### Torus Volume and Total Surface Area
$$V = 2 \pi^2 R r^2, \quad A = 4 \pi^2 R r$$
By Pappus of Alexandria's centroid theorems (Book VII of the *Collection*, c. 340 CE), revolving a planar circular cross-section of minor tube radius $r$ (area $\pi r^2$, perimeter $2\pi r$) around an external coplanar axis at major centroid radius $R$ ($R \ge r$) sweeps out a volume equal to the cross-sectional area times the centroid path length $2\pi R$, and a surface area equal to the perimeter times $2\pi R$. Because inward curvature on the inner equator ($R - r$) exactly cancels outward curvature on the outer equator ($R + r$), the torus behaves metrically like a straight cylinder of radius $r$ and length $2\pi R$, governing toroidal inductors, O-ring elastomer seals, and tokamak fusion vessels.

#### Heron's Formula for Arbitrary Triangle Area
$$A = \sqrt{s(s - a)(s - b)(s - c)}, \quad s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}$$
Recorded by Heron of Alexandria in Book I of his *Metrica* (c. 60 CE), this intrinsic distance formula determines the planar area $A$ of any triangle directly from its three edge lengths $a, b, c$ and semiperimeter $s = (a + b + c)/2$ without requiring an interior angle or dropped altitude. Each factor $(s - a), (s - b), (s - c)$ represents the tangent segment from a vertex to the inscribed circle of inradius $r = A / s$, and their product vanishes whenever the triangle degenerates into a collinear segment ($a + b = c$). Computing semiperimeter $s$ once, storing it in register `S`, and forming the four-term product under the radical (`a [ENTER] b [+] c [+] 2 [÷] [STO] S a [-] [RCL] S b [-] [×] [RCL] S c [-] [×] [RCL] S [×] [√x]`) for the classic $(13, 14, 15)$ Heronian triangle ($s = 21.0$, factors $21 \times 8 \times 7 \times 6 = 7056$) gives `84.000`.

#### Law of Cosines for Arbitrary Triangle
$$c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 - 2 a b \cos C}$$
Generalized from Book II, Propositions 12–13 of Euclid's *Elements* by the Persian astronomer Jamshīd al-Kāshī in 1427, the Law of Cosines resolves the third side $c$ of any oblique triangle from two adjacent sides $a, b$ and their included angle $C$ (degrees). Subtracting the Euclidean inner-product projection $2ab\cos C$ from the Pythagorean sum $a^2 + b^2$ accounts for acute ($C < 90^\circ$, where $\cos C > 0$ shortens $c$) and obtuse ($C > 90^\circ$, where $\cos C < 0$ lengthens $c$) vertex geometry, collapsing to $c = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}$ at $C = 90^\circ$. In `[DEG]` mode, summing $a^2 + b^2$ in Register $Y$, subtracting $2ab\cos C$, and taking `[√x]` (`a [↰] [x²] b [↰] [x²] [+] 2 [ENTER] a [×] b [×] C [COS] [×] [-] [√x]`) for $a = 18.0, b = 25.0, C = 62.0^\circ$ returns `22.945`.

#### Great Circle Spherical Distance (Haversine Formula)
$$d = 2 R \arcsin\left(\sqrt{\sin^2\left(\frac{\Delta\phi}{2}\right) + \cos\phi_1 \cos\phi_2 \sin^2\left(\frac{\Delta\lambda}{2}\right)}\right)$$
Introduced by James Inman in his 1835 *Navigation and Nautical Astronomy*, the haversine formula computes the shortest geodesic arc $d$ across a sphere of mean Earth radius $R = 6371.0\text{ km}$ between coordinates $(\phi_1, \lambda_1)$ and $(\phi_2, \lambda_2)$ using half-versed sines $\text{hav}(\theta) = \sin^2(\theta/2)$ of the latitude difference $\Delta\phi = \phi_2 - \phi_1$ and longitude difference $\Delta\lambda = \lambda_2 - \lambda_1$. Expressing central angle entirely in terms of $\sin^2(\Delta/2)$ avoids the severe floating-point cancellation that plagues the spherical law of cosines $\arccos(\sin\phi_1\sin\phi_2 + \cos\phi_1\cos\phi_2\cos\Delta\lambda)$ when two waypoints lie only meters or kilometers apart ($\cos\theta \approx 0.99999999$).

In `[DEG]` mode, evaluating the two haversine terms from the inside out (`phi2 [ENTER] phi1 [-] 2 [÷] [SIN] [↰] [x²] phi1 [COS] phi2 [COS] [×] lam2 [ENTER] lam1 [-] 2 [÷] [SIN] [↰] [x²] [×] [+] [√x] [↰] [ASIN] 2 [×] 6371.0 [×]`) from New York ($40.7128^\circ\text{N}, 74.0060^\circ\text{W}$) to London ($51.5074^\circ\text{N}, 0.1278^\circ\text{W}$) yields `5570.2` $\text{km}$ ($3461.2\text{ miles}$).

#### Circular Sector Area and Arc Length
$$s = r \theta, \quad A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 \theta \quad (\theta\text{ in radians})$$
Because radian measure defines a central angle $\theta$ (in $\text{rad}$) as the dimensionless ratio of subtended arc length $s$ to radius $r$, a circular sector occupying fraction $\theta / (2\pi)$ of a complete turn has arc length $s = (\theta / 2\pi)(2\pi r) = r\theta$ and enclosed pie-slice area $A = (\theta / 2\pi)(\pi r^2) = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$. By a direct structural parallel to linear kinematics ($v = at$ and $x = \frac{1}{2}at^2$), integrating circumferential arc length $r\theta$ radially from $0$ to $r$ produces $\int_0^r \rho\theta\,d\rho = \frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$. Multiplying `r [ENTER] theta [×]` for arc length or `r [↰] [x²] theta [×] 2 [÷]` for sector area at $r = 12.0\text{ cm}$ and $\theta = 1.047198\text{ rad}$ ($60.0^\circ$, convert via `60 [↱] [▸RAD]`) yields Arc Length = `12.566` $\text{cm}$ and Sector Area = `75.398` $\text{cm}^2$.

#### Circular Segment Area
$$A = \frac{1}{2} r^2 (\theta - \sin\theta) \quad (\theta\text{ in radians})$$
A circular segment—the region bounded by a secant chord and its subtended arc of central angle $\theta$ (in radians) on a circle of radius $r$—is obtained by subtracting the area of the central isosceles triangle $\frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta$ from the full circular sector $\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta$. Civil and process engineers rely on this difference to calibrate the liquid volume inside partially filled horizontal cylindrical storage tanks and storm sewers as a function of wetted angle $\theta = 2\arccos((r - h)/r)$. In `[RAD]` mode, duplicating $\theta$ with `[ENTER]` to form $\theta - \sin\theta$ before multiplying by $r^2 / 2$ (`theta [ENTER] [SIN] [-] r [↰] [x²] [×] 2 [÷]`) for $r = 8.0\text{ m}$ and $\theta = 1.250\text{ rad}$ gives `9.633` $\text{m}^2$.

#### Circular Annulus & Annular Sector Area
$$A = \pi (R^2 - r^2) = \pi (R - r)(R + r), \quad A_{\text{sector}} = \frac{\theta}{2} (R - r)(R + r)$$
The planar ring (annulus) between two concentric circles of outer radius $R$ and inner bore radius $r$ has area $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$, while a sector subtending central angle $\theta$ ($\text{rad}$) encloses $A_{\text{sector}} = \frac{\theta}{2}(R^2 - r^2)$. Factoring the difference of squares as $(R - r)(R + r)$ reveals that the annulus area equals the radial wall thickness $w = R - r$ multiplied by the mean circumference $2\pi r_{\text{mean}} = \pi(R + r)$, and prevents loss of significant digits when evaluating thin-walled pipe cross-sections where $R \approx r$. #### Ellipse Area & Ramanujan's Second Perimeter Approximation
$$A = \pi a b, \quad h = \frac{(a - b)^2}{(a + b)^2}, \quad P \approx \pi (a + b) \left[ 1 + \frac{3h}{10 + \sqrt{4 - 3h}} \right]$$
Because an ellipse of semimajor axis $a$ and semiminor axis $b$ ($a \ge b$) is a uniform vertical scaling of a circle of radius $a$ by the aspect ratio $b/a$, its enclosed area scales exact circle area $\pi a^2$ to $A = \pi a b$. By contrast, its arc-length perimeter $P = 4a E(e)$ requires the complete elliptic integral of the second kind and admits no elementary closed form; however, Srinivasa Ramanujan's 1914 second rational approximation in terms of the symmetric oblateness parameter $h = (a - b)^2 / (a + b)^2$ matches the exact elliptic integral up to the $h^5$ Maclaurin term (accurate to better than $0.0004\%$ even at aspect ratios of $3:1$).

#### Parabolic Segment Area (Archimedes' Quadrature)
$$A = \frac{2}{3} b h$$
In *Quadrature of the Parabola* (c. 240 BCE)—the earliest known summation of an infinite geometric series ($1 + \frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{16} + \dots = \frac{4}{3}$)—Archimedes proved that the planar region bounded by a parabola and a chord of width $b$ with perpendicular vertex sagitta $h$ encloses exactly four-thirds the area of the inscribed triangle ($\frac{1}{2}bh$), or two-thirds the area of the circumscribing rectangle ($bh$). Structural engineers use this exact $\frac{2}{3}bh$ factor daily when integrating parabolic shear-stress distributions across rectangular beams and parabolic bending-moment diagrams under uniform loading.
